AI.tldr: OASIS is a simulation-data-driven framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that uses 3D generative models to reconstruct object assets from real images, collects trajectories via simulation teleoperation, augments them with domain randomizations, and trains a hierarchical visuomotor policy that outperforms real-robot teleoperation data under zero-shot deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing data sources for humanoid loco-manipulation force a tradeoff between trajectory quality (real-world teleoperation) and scalability (requires physical space, time-consuming resets). Simulation offers a way to produce clean, embodiment-aligned data at scale without physical hardware.
AI.method: OASIS: 1) Automatically reconstructs realistic 3D object assets from real-world images using a generative model. 2) Collects trajectories via teleoperation in simulation. 3) Augments trajectories with diverse domain randomizations (lighting, environment) in post-processing. 4) Trains a hierarchical visuomotor policy for humanoid loco-manipulation.
AI.result: Under zero-shot deployment on a real humanoid robot, the policy trained on OASIS simulation data achieves higher success rates on most tasks than that trained on real-robot teleoperation data.
AI.conclusion: Simulation data with broad domain randomization can surpass real-robot teleoperation data for training humanoid loco-manipulation policies, because real data fails to capture the lighting and environmental variations that simulation rendering provides.

title: Decision-Aware Memory Cards: Counterfactual-Inspired Context Selection and Compression for Tool-Using LLM Agents
comment: 15 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/stephen-guan-researcher/CICL; Qwen-QLoRA adapter is available at https://huggingface.co/XinyuGuan/CICL
summary: Tool-using LLM agents often fail not because relevant text is absent, but because decisive evidence is not selected, compressed, or surfaced at action time. We present CICL, a decision-aware context layer that turns instance evidence into a context graph, routes deterministic, Opus-assisted, Qwen, Codex/GPT-5.5, and Qwen-QLoRA judgments through a shared eight-field schema, scores units by action shift, outcome uplift, necessity, and negative-transfer risk, and packs high-utility evidence as typed memory cards for a budgeted agent. The design separates the measured decision signal from the judge model, so frontier annotation, local surrogates, and lightweight rankers can be compared under one auditable protocol. Empirically, CICL yields a concrete open-benchmark gain while exposing its limits. On 50 SWE-bench Verified file-retrieval instances, direct Qwen3.6-plus reranking of BM25 top-50 candidates raises hit@1 from 0.58 to 0.78 and MRR@10 from 0.634 to 0.790, with all 2,500 judgments parseable. Controlled diagnostics show action-criticality: at budget 120, CICL reaches F1 0.620 on v1 and 0.425 on v3, and removing the top-utility semantic v3 unit collapses F1 to 0.000. Supplementary checks add Qwen-QLoRA agreement over 710 candidates, a small 200-label real-code Opus-assisted signal, and a three-instance patch smoke validating retrieval-to-patch plumbing without claiming official SWE-bench success. RepoBench-R summaries still beat cards, and compact rankers do not yet replace the heuristic. CICL contributes a reproducible measurement and selection layer for decision-critical context, not an end-to-end coding-agent repair claim.

AI.tldr: CICL is a decision-aware context layer that selects critical evidence for LLM agents using a shared eight-field schema, improving retrieval hit rates on SWE-bench from 0.58 to 0.78 hit@1, while separating measurement from the judge model for auditable comparison.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents fail not because relevant text is absent, but because decisive evidence is not selected, compressed, or surfaced at action time.
AI.method: CICL converts instance evidence into a context graph, routes judgments (Opus, Qwen, Codex/GPT-5.5, Qwen-QLoRA) through a shared eight-field schema, scores units by action shift, outcome uplift, necessity, and negative-transfer risk, then packs high-utility evidence as typed memory cards for budgeted agents.
AI.result: On 50 SWE-bench Verified instances: hit@1 improves from 0.58 to 0.78, MRR@10 from 0.634 to 0.790 with all 2,500 judgments parseable. At budget 120, CICL reaches F1 0.620 (v1) and 0.425 (v3); removing top-utility v3 unit collapses F1 to 0.000.
AI.conclusion: CICL contributes a reproducible measurement and selection layer for decision-critical context, not an end-to-end coding-agent repair claim.

title: FAWAM: Force-Aware World Action Models for Closed-Loop Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Force signals provide critical interaction cues for contact-rich robotic manipulation. However, existing methods mostly use force as an additional observation modality, without fully exploiting its role in modeling future interaction dynamics or guiding execution-time feedback correction. In this paper, we propose FAWAM, a force-aware world action model that incorporates force information at three levels: perception, prediction, and closed-loop execution. FAWAM first encodes historical 6-axis force/torque signals to modulate action generation, then jointly predicts future actions and end-effector wrenches to explicitly model contact evolution. It further introduces a residual correction module that uses the predicted wrench trajectory as an execution-time reference to refine actions online based on real-time force feedback. Real-world experiments across multiple contact-rich tasks show that FAWAM improves the average success rate by 36.25% over vision-only baselines and 21.25% over existing force-aware baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of our force-aware framework for robust contact-rich manipulation.

AI.tldr: FAWAM is a force-aware world action model that integrates force information at three levels (perception, prediction, closed-loop execution) for contact-rich robotic manipulation, achieving 36.25% higher success rate than vision-only baselines and 21.25% over force-aware baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat force as an additional observation modality without fully exploiting its role in modeling future interaction dynamics or guiding execution-time feedback correction.
AI.method: FAWAM incorporates force at three levels: (1) encodes historical 6-axis force/torque signals to modulate action generation, (2) jointly predicts future actions and end-effector wrenches to model contact evolution, (3) uses a residual correction module that leverages predicted wrench trajectory for online action refinement via real-time force feedback.
AI.result: Real-world experiments show 36.25% average success rate improvement over vision-only baselines and 21.25% improvement over existing force-aware baselines across multiple contact-rich tasks.
AI.conclusion: The force-aware framework effectively integrates force at perception, prediction, and execution levels, demonstrating robust contact-rich manipulation.

title: Online Agent-as-a-Judge: Situation-Generating Evaluation for Interactive Agents
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Trustworthy AI for Good
summary: Evaluating LLM-powered interactive social agents is challenging because socially relevant behaviors depend not only on isolated outputs, but also on prior interactions, social roles, and downstream actions. Existing methods typically allow a target agent to act freely in an environment and then score the resulting trajectory. However, this passive setup can miss capabilities that only become observable under specific social circumstances; for example, conflict handling may remain untested if no disagreement arises. We propose Online Agent-as-a-Judge, a situation-generating evaluation framework for interactive social agents. Online Agent-as-a-Judge deploys an in-world evaluator agent that interacts with the target agent through the environment's native dialogue and action protocol, actively eliciting situations relevant to the evaluation criteria. The resulting trajectories provide evidence for assessing both immediate responses and subsequent behavior. In a life-simulation environment with $32$ designer-authored social criteria, Online Agent-as-a-Judge improves criteria coverage and agreement with human labels, yielding more reliable evidence-grounded evaluations of behaviors that passive methods can leave unobserved.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Online Agent-as-a-Judge, an evaluation framework where an in-world evaluator agent actively interacts with a target social agent to elicit specific social situations (e.g., conflict) that passive observation would miss, improving criteria coverage and alignment with human judgments.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation methods for LLM-powered social agents are passive—they let the target agent act freely and score the trajectory—but this misses capabilities that only surface under specific social circumstances (e.g., conflict handling when no disagreement occurs naturally). A more proactive evaluation approach is needed.
AI.method: Online Agent-as-a-Judge deploys an in-world evaluator agent that interacts with the target agent via the environment's native dialogue and action protocol, actively eliciting situations relevant to predefined evaluation criteria. The resulting trajectories provide evidence for assessing both immediate and subsequent behaviors.
AI.result: In a life-simulation environment with 32 designer-authored social criteria, the framework improves criteria coverage and agreement with human labels compared to passive methods.
AI.conclusion: Active, situation-generating evaluation via an in-world evaluator agent yields more reliable, evidence-grounded assessments of socially relevant behaviors that passive methods would leave unobserved.

title: Real-IKEA: Physical Fidelity is the Prerequisite for Robust Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation robustness often founders on the physics gap between simplified simulations and the resistance-laden real world. In this work, we emphasize that physical realism in articulated interaction is an important ingredient for robust policy learning. We present Real-IKEA, a dataset and simulation framework designed with physical accuracy as a first-class goal. Real-IKEA provides 1,079 articulated asset configurations, derived from 83 authentic IKEA handles and knobs processed through a meticulous six-step physical workflow. For contact-geometry accuracy, we introduce a bidirectional surface-deviation metric to quantify collision meshes. For dynamics realism, we establish resistance-calibrated configurations that vary damping and friction. Crucially, we demonstrate through a Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy that high-fidelity assets enable the discovery of robust "hooking" and "levering" strategies that prioritize mechanical advantage over fragile friction-pulling. Together, these results position Real-IKEA as a critical benchmark for developing manipulation policies capable of human-level robustness in articulated object tasks.

AI.tldr: Real-IKEA is a physically accurate dataset and simulation framework with 1,079 articulated asset configurations from 83 IKEA handles/knobs, featuring bidirectional surface-deviation metrics for contact geometry and resistance-calibrated dynamics, enabling RL policies to learn robust mechanical-advantage strategies (hooking/levering) rather than fragile friction-pulling.
AI.motivation: Robotic manipulation robustness suffers from the physics gap between simplified simulations and real-world resistance; physical realism in articulated interaction is essential for robust policy learning.
AI.method: Created 1,079 articulated asset configurations from 83 IKEA handles/knobs via a six-step physical workflow; introduced bidirectional surface-deviation metric for collision mesh accuracy; established resistance-calibrated configurations with varying damping and friction.
AI.result: RL policies trained on high-fidelity Real-IKEA assets discover robust "hooking" and "levering" strategies that prioritize mechanical advantage over fragile friction-pulling.
AI.conclusion: Real-IKEA serves as a critical benchmark for developing manipulation policies with human-level robustness in articulated object tasks.

title: SciTrace: Trajectory-Aware Safety Reasoning for Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: LLM-based scientific agents have shown strong capacity for autonomous research, yet their safety layers remain structurally divorced from core reasoning: they inspect pipeline outputs rather than shaping the deliberation that produces them. This separation opens two failure modes: safety signals accumulated at one stage are discarded before the next, and sequences of individually benign tool calls can compose into harmful outcomes that no single-step filter detects. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{SciTrace}, a framework that weaves safety reasoning into every stage of the scientific agent pipeline. SciTrace couples two complementary mechanisms: a \textit{Safety-Intrinsic Reasoning Loop} (SIR) that maintains a cumulative risk state across the Thinker, Experimenter, Writer, and Reviewer stages through joint task-and-safety deliberation, and a \textit{Compositional Tool-Chain Verifier} (CTV) that performs trajectory-aware safety checks before execution, catching risks that surface only across multi-step tool sequences. Evaluated on 240 high-risk research tasks and 120 tool-related risk tasks spanning six scientific domains, SciTrace achieves state-of-the-art (\textbf{SOTA}) safety among compared frameworks across four backbone models: it consistently improves tool call safety and adversarial robustness while preserving scientific output quality, and it uncovers \textbf{78.8\%} of the compositional tool-chain escapes that single-step monitors miss. The project website is available at https://opensciagent.github.io/SciTrace/.

AI.tldr: SciTrace is a safety framework for LLM-based scientific agents that integrates safety reasoning into every pipeline stage via a Safety-Intrinsic Reasoning Loop (cumulative risk state across stages) and a Compositional Tool-Chain Verifier (trajectory-aware pre-execution checks), achieving SOTA safety across four backbone models on 240 high-risk research tasks and 120 tool-risk tasks, catching 78.8% of compositional tool-chain escapes missed by single-step monitors.
AI.motivation: Existing safety layers in LLM-based scientific agents are structurally divorced from core reasoning—they inspect pipeline outputs rather than shaping the deliberation that produces them—leading to two failure modes: safety signals accumulated at one stage are discarded before the next, and sequences of individually benign tool calls can compose into harmful outcomes that no single-step filter detects.
AI.method: SciTrace couples two complementary mechanisms: (1) a Safety-Intrinsic Reasoning Loop (SIR) that maintains a cumulative risk state across the Thinker, Experimenter, Writer, and Reviewer stages through joint task-and-safety deliberation; and (2) a Compositional Tool-Chain Verifier (CTV) that performs trajectory-aware safety checks before execution, catching risks that surface only across multi-step tool sequences.
AI.result: Evaluated on 240 high-risk research tasks and 120 tool-related risk tasks across six scientific domains, SciTrace achieves state-of-the-art safety among compared frameworks across four backbone models, consistently improving tool call safety and adversarial robustness while preserving scientific output quality, and uncovers 78.8% of compositional tool-chain escapes that single-step monitors miss.
AI.conclusion: Integrating safety reasoning intrinsically into every stage of the scientific agent pipeline (rather than post-hoc inspection) effectively mitigates both cumulative risk loss across stages and compositional tool-chain risks, achieving superior safety without sacrificing scientific output quality.

title: HARBOR: A Harness Framework for Agentic Robot Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a powerful paradigm for robot learning, particularly in sim-to-real settings, but its broader adoption remains limited by the engineering pipeline surrounding the algorithms. Building tasks, shaping rewards, and tuning hyperparameters require substantial expert effort, making RL workflows costly and difficult to scale. We introduce HARBOR, an agentic framework that frames robot RL automation as a harness-engineering problem: given a simulator codebase and a task specification, it automates the workflow from environment setup to policy training in simulation. HARBOR decomposes such high-level objectives into bounded stages executed by specialized agents through standardized commands, persistent artifacts, executable gates, and reusable knowledge, and scales iteration via decentralized parallel trials and experience learning across runs. We evaluate HARBOR across 6 benchmarks and 16 tasks in total, spanning manipulation, locomotion, and bimanual dexterous control. We demonstrate that HARBOR automates the simulation RL workflow end-to-end, designs rewards, tunes algorithms to match or improve over default configurations, and reduces engineering effort at practical token and wall-clock cost; the resulting policies can also be transferred to real robots.

AI.tldr: HARBOR is an agentic framework that automates the entire robot reinforcement learning workflow in simulation, from environment setup to policy training, by decomposing tasks into specialized agents with standardized commands and reusable knowledge. It matches or improves over default configurations across 16 tasks spanning manipulation, locomotion, and bimanual dexterous control, with real-robot transfer capability.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for robotics requires substantial expert effort for building tasks, shaping rewards, and tuning hyperparameters, making RL workflows costly and difficult to scale. The goal is to automate this engineering pipeline to reduce human burden.
AI.method: HARBOR frames RL automation as a harness-engineering problem. It decomposes high-level objectives into bounded stages executed by specialized agents using standardized commands, persistent artifacts, executable gates, and reusable knowledge. It scales via decentralized parallel trials and experience learning across runs.
AI.result: Evaluated across 6 benchmarks and 16 tasks (manipulation, locomotion, bimanual dexterous control), HARBOR automates the simulation RL workflow end-to-end, designs rewards, tunes algorithms to match or improve over default configurations, reduces engineering effort at practical token and wall-clock cost, and enables real-robot transfer.
AI.conclusion: HARBOR demonstrates that agentic automation of the RL engineering pipeline is feasible and effective, reducing human effort while maintaining or improving policy performance, with practical computational cost and sim-to-real transfer capability.

title: When No Answer Is Correct: Diagnosing Absent Answer Detection for MLLMs in Video Understanding
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial advancements in video understanding, yet the reliability of their responses remains underexplored. This work presents a diagnostic study of absent answer detection for MLLMs in video understanding, where the correct answer is deliberately excluded from the candidate set and a reliable model is expected to recognize that no valid option exists. We evaluate the absent answer detection behavior under three settings: multiple-choice questions augmented with an ``None of the Above'' option, open-ended generation with a detection instruction, and standard evaluation without any guidance. Across a diverse set of models and benchmarks, we find that MLLMs overwhelmingly select plausible distractors rather than detecting the absent answer. This failure is more pronounced in temporal reasoning tasks and worsens with denser frame sampling. We further explore chain-of-thought prompting as a mitigation strategy and find that while it substantially improves detection rates, performance remains unsatisfactory, suggesting that prompting-based strategies alone are insufficient to fully address this limitation. These findings expose a systematic failure in absent answer detection and highlight the need for explicit detection mechanisms in multimodal systems.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) fail to detect when the correct answer is missing from candidate options in video understanding tasks. MLLMs tend to pick plausible distractors instead of recognizing that no valid answer exists, especially in temporal reasoning and with dense frame sampling. Chain-of-thought prompting helps but remains insufficient, revealing a systematic limitation that requires explicit detection mechanisms.
AI.motivation: While MLLMs have advanced in video understanding, their reliability in recognizing when no correct answer is available remains unexplored. The authors aim to diagnose this absent answer detection failure, which is critical for trustworthy deployment.
AI.method: The authors evaluate MLLMs under three settings: (1) multiple-choice with a "None of the Above" option, (2) open-ended generation with a detection instruction, and (3) standard evaluation without guidance. They test across diverse models and benchmarks, varying frame sampling density and using chain-of-thought prompting as a mitigation strategy.
AI.result: MLLMs overwhelmingly select plausible distractors instead of detecting absent answers. The failure is more severe in temporal reasoning tasks and worsens with denser frame sampling. Chain-of-thought prompting improves detection rates but performance remains unsatisfactory, indicating prompting alone is insufficient.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a systematic failure in absent answer detection in MLLMs for video understanding, highlighting the need for explicit detection mechanisms beyond prompting-based strategies.

title: PhysGraph: A Physics-aware 3D Scene Graph for Perception and Reasoning
summary: To perform a wide range of daily tasks, robots need to construct a 3D representation that is semantically rich, physically grounded, and structured enough to support task planning and affordance prediction. However, existing approaches primarily focus on semantic retrieval, often overlooking physical and kinematic factors. Methods that attempt to model physical properties typically rely on narrow training sets or single-object modeling, limiting scalability and generalization across diverse object types. To address these challenges, we present PhysGraph, a framework that unifies symbolic reasoning with structured 3D geometry to model kinematic and physical properties in cluttered scenes. Given RGB-D observations, PhysGraph reconstructs object-centric 3D geometry and associates object instances across views. It then decomposes objects into functional parts and infers materials and articulations through visual reasoning. Evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets, PhysGraph achieves state-of-the-art results in semantic segmentation, multi-object mass estimation, and articulation prediction. With its simple yet effective design, PhysGraph produces physically consistent and semantically structured scene graphs, serving as a structured 3D representation for downstream tasks such as constraint-aware 3D affordance prediction and real-to-sim transfer, both of which are demonstrated in our experiments.

AI.tldr: PhysGraph is a framework that unifies symbolic reasoning with structured 3D geometry to model kinematic and physical properties of objects in cluttered scenes, achieving state-of-the-art results in semantic segmentation, mass estimation, and articulation prediction for downstream robotics tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D representations for robotics lack physical and kinematic grounding; they primarily focus on semantic retrieval and fail to model physical properties like mass, articulation, and material, limiting task planning and affordance prediction.
AI.method: PhysGraph takes RGB-D observations, reconstructs object-centric 3D geometry, associates instances across views, decomposes objects into functional parts, and infers materials and articulations via visual reasoning to build physically consistent scene graphs.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on synthetic and real-world datasets for semantic segmentation, multi-object mass estimation, and articulation prediction; demonstrates effectiveness in constraint-aware 3D affordance prediction and real-to-sim transfer.
AI.conclusion: PhysGraph provides a simple yet effective structured 3D representation that is semantically rich and physically grounded, serving as a unified framework to support downstream robotics tasks requiring physical and kinematic understanding.

title: Traxia: A Framework for Verifiable, Agent-Native Scientific Publishing
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Preprint. Under active development. Comments welcome
summary: Verifiability, attribution, and reproducibility are foundational requirements of scientific knowledge, yet current publishing infrastructure does not enforce them at scale. We introduce Traxia, an agent-native scientific publishing framework in which AI research agents publish verifiable papers, build reputational identities, peer-review one another, and collaborate with humans in a shared provenance model. Traxia treats agents as first-class epistemic participants: every paper carries a reasoning trace, every claim a confidence interval, every agent a cryptographically signed identity, and every collaboration an immutable contribution log. We formalise five components: Agent Identity and Registry, Verifiable Publishing Layer, four-tier Peer Review Protocol, Reputation and Staking Engine, and a Knowledge Graph with contradiction detection. The framework targets reproducibility failure, provenance opacity, and exclusion of Global South research capacity. This paper presents architectural foundations and formal specifications only; it does not report empirical results. Evaluation and deeper component studies will follow in subsequent papers. A prototype partially implements core formalisms; the full system remains under active development.

AI.tldr: Traxia is an agent-native scientific publishing framework where AI research agents publish verifiable papers, build reputational identities, peer-review each other, and collaborate with humans, featuring cryptographic signing, reasoning traces, confidence intervals, immutable contribution logs, and a four-tier peer review protocol to address reproducibility, provenance, and global equity issues.
AI.motivation: Current publishing infrastructure does not enforce verifiability, attribution, and reproducibility at scale, and suffers from reproducibility failure, provenance opacity, and exclusion of Global South research capacity.
AI.method: Traxia formalizes five components: Agent Identity and Registry, Verifiable Publishing Layer, four-tier Peer Review Protocol, Reputation and Staking Engine, and Knowledge Graph with contradiction detection. It treats agents as first-class epistemic participants with reasoning traces, confidence intervals, cryptographically signed identities, and immutable contribution logs.
AI.result: This paper presents architectural foundations and formal specifications only; no empirical results are reported. A prototype partially implements core formalisms; the full system is under active development.
AI.conclusion: Traxia proposes a framework for verifiable, attributed, and reproducible AI-native scientific publishing, with evaluation and deeper component studies to follow in subsequent papers.

title: Latent Diffusion Policy: Shaping Latent Spaces for Diffusion-Based Robotic Manipulation
summary: Diffusion-based visuomotor policies operating directly in raw action spaces conflate scene comprehension with trajectory generation within a single denoising process. The resulting velocity field must simultaneously encode scene information and generate precise trajectories, increasing learning complexity and limiting performance on tasks demanding precise temporal coordination across multiple arms. To simplify this joint learning problem, we introduce Latent Diffusion Policy (LDP), a two-stage framework performing flow matching in a deliberately shaped latent space. By absorbing scene understanding into an observation-conditioned CVAE encoder, LDP concentrates the conditional distribution of each observation. Consequently, the flow model avoids implicitly resolving scene-dependent structures; instead, it generates within a pre-concentrated distribution featuring a smoother velocity field, simplifying learning from limited demonstrations. Furthermore, to capture temporal dependencies among latent tokens, LDP trains with per-token diffusion forcing and employs staircase inference sampling to resolve the resulting distributional mismatch. We also propose reconstruction FID (rFID) as a lightweight proxy predicting downstream task success solely from latent space statistics. On coordination-intensive tasks from RoboTwin 2.0, LDP outperforms DP3 by a substantial margin and transfers effectively to real-world bimanual deployments.

AI.tldr: LDP is a two-stage framework that separates scene understanding from trajectory generation by using a CVAE to shape a latent space, enabling a smoother flow matching process that outperforms DP3 on coordination-intensive bimanual tasks.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based visuomotor policies conflate scene comprehension with trajectory generation in a single denoising process, increasing learning complexity and limiting performance on tasks requiring precise temporal coordination across multiple arms.
AI.method: LDP employs a two-stage framework: (1) an observation-conditioned CVAE encoder absorbs scene understanding to concentrate the conditional distribution, and (2) a flow matching model generates trajectories within this shaped latent space with a smoother velocity field. It uses per-token diffusion forcing during training and staircase inference sampling to resolve distributional mismatch, plus reconstruction FID (rFID) as a lightweight proxy for downstream task success.
AI.result: On coordination-intensive tasks from RoboTwin 2.0, LDP outperforms DP3 by a substantial margin and transfers effectively to real-world bimanual deployments.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling scene understanding from trajectory generation via a shaped latent space simplifies learning and significantly improves performance on temporally coordinated multi-arm tasks.

title: From Validator Selection to Portfolio Collection Optimization in Proof-of-Stake Blockchains
summary: We consider a problem arising in proof-of-stake blockchain environments, where agents called nominators select validators - entities responsible for maintaining the blockchain's physical infrastructure. The selection process is inherently subjective and multi-criterial and combines with the fact that nominators commonly operate through multiple accounts. This gives rise to a portfolio selection problem, where agents seek to distribute their nominations across accounts to diversify risk. We propose a decision support framework to optimize this selection by simultaneously maximizing two objectives: the expected utility of the validators likely to be allocated, representing portfolio quality and profitability, and the expected entropy of the allocation, representing diversification and risk mitigation across stashes. Validator utilities are derived using an original active preference learning procedure based on multi-attribute value theory, with emphasis on top-ranked validators. The resulting bi-objective optimization problem is solved with a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm and, to support the final choice, we introduce an interactive binary search navigation procedure that guides the nominator through the front and identifies a satisfactory trade-off with only a few questions. Numerical experiments examine the optimization strategies, while an expert assessment involving five experienced nominators confirms the approach's practical relevance and usefulness.

AI.tldr: A decision support framework for optimal validator selection in proof-of-stake blockchains, balancing portfolio quality and diversification through bi-objective optimization with active preference learning.
AI.motivation: Nominators in proof-of-stake blockchains face a complex, multi-criteria portfolio selection problem when choosing validators, especially when operating through multiple accounts. The goal is to simultaneously optimize portfolio quality (expected utility of allocated validators) and diversification (expected entropy of allocation) to mitigate risk.
AI.method: 1) Active preference learning using multi-attribute value theory to derive validator utilities with emphasis on top-ranked validators. 2) Bi-objective optimization solved with a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. 3) Interactive binary search navigation procedure to guide the nominator to a satisfactory trade-off on the Pareto front.
AI.result: Numerical experiments examined optimization strategies. An expert assessment involving five experienced nominators confirmed the approach's practical relevance and usefulness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses the subjective, multi-criteria validator selection problem in proof-of-stake systems, providing a practical tool for nominators to balance profitability and risk diversification across their stashes.

title: Language as a Sensor: Calibrated Spatial Belief Estimation in 3D Scenes from Natural Language
summary: Robots deployed in human-centric environments routinely receive natural-language descriptions of spatial information ("I left my backpack on the table") that reference parts of the world beyond their perceptual field of view. Traditional metric-semantic mapping ignores this signal, while off-the-shelf multimodal models remain limited in 3D spatial reasoning and are not directly amenable to fusion with other sensor modalities. To convert language observations into a calibrated spatial distribution, we train a Language Sensor Model (LSM) that maps each utterance and its scene-graph context to a multimodal distribution, with mixture weights encoding referential ambiguity (e.g., "which table") and component covariances encoding spatial uncertainty (e.g., where "on the table" the target lies). We then introduce VL-Map (Vision-Language Metric-Semantic Mapping), a probabilistic framework that treats these language predictions as stochastic observations and fuses them with onboard perception within a unified belief map. On the VLA-3D benchmark as well as on a real-world mobile robot, LSM is the only language predictor whose covariance estimates remain within the calibrated regime; fused into VL-Map, it leads to more accurate predictions of the target object location (~70% more probability mass on the true target compared to the strongest foundation-model baseline).

AI.tldr: The paper introduces VL-Map, a probabilistic mapping framework that uses a trained Language Sensor Model (LSM) to convert natural-language spatial descriptions into calibrated spatial distributions, which are then fused with onboard perception for improved 3D target localization in human-centric environments.
AI.motivation: Robots operating in human-centric environments receive natural-language spatial descriptions (e.g., "I left my backpack on the table") that refer to objects/areas beyond their perceptual field of view. Traditional metric-semantic mapping ignores this linguistic signal, and existing multimodal models lack 3D spatial reasoning capabilities and cannot easily fuse with other sensor modalities.
AI.method: The authors train a Language Sensor Model (LSM) that maps utterances and scene-graph context to a multimodal distribution, where mixture weights encode referential ambiguity and component covariances encode spatial uncertainty. They then propose VL-Map (Vision-Language Metric-Semantic Mapping), a probabilistic framework that treats language predictions as stochastic observations and fuses them with onboard perception within a unified belief map.
AI.result: On the VLA-3D benchmark and a real-world mobile robot, LSM is the only language predictor with calibrated covariance estimates. When fused into VL-Map, it achieves ~70% more probability mass on the true target object location compared to the strongest foundation-model baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LSM and VL-Map framework effectively leverage natural-language spatial descriptions as calibrated probabilistic observations, significantly improving 3D target localization accuracy by fusing language with onboard perception in a principled manner.

title: Beyond Agent Architecture: Execution Assumptions and Reproducibility in LLM-Based Trading Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems are increasingly proposed for financial trading, yet their reported performance remains difficult to compare because studies vary in data provenance, temporal split discipline, execution timing, turnover treatment, and transaction-cost modeling. This article presents a targeted topical review and reproducibility audit of execution realism in LLM-based trading research. A coded evidence matrix covering 30 trade-relevant primary studies is used to assess point-in-time controls, split transparency, held-out evaluation, cost and turnover treatment, execution semantics, universe definition, and artifact release. Across the audited sample, architecture reporting is generally clearer than the evaluation assumptions needed to judge whether a trading result is economically interpretable or reproducible. A 10-equity worked example is included only as a methodological scaffold to illustrate how explicit friction and timing choices can materially compress active-strategy results. The main conclusion is that the next useful step for LLM trading research is not only better agent design, but also clearer reporting standards for execution realism, reproducibility, and evaluation comparability.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews 30 LLM-based trading studies and finds that while architecture details are reported clearly, evaluation assumptions about execution realism (timing, costs, turnover) are poorly documented, making results incomparable and economically uninterpretable. The authors call for standardized reporting of execution realism and reproducibility rather than just better agent design.
AI.motivation: LLM-based trading research lacks comparability because studies use different data sources, time splits, cost models, and execution assumptions, making it impossible to judge whether reported results are economically meaningful or reproducible.
AI.method: A targeted topical review and reproducibility audit using a coded evidence matrix covering 30 trade-relevant primary studies. Assessed dimensions include point-in-time controls, split transparency, held-out evaluation, cost/turnover treatment, execution semantics, universe definition, and artifact release. A 10-equity worked example illustrates how friction/timing choices compress strategy results.
AI.result: Architecture reporting is clearer than evaluation assumptions across the audited sample. The 10-equity example demonstrates that explicit friction and timing choices materially compress active-strategy results.
AI.conclusion: The needed step forward is not just better agent design but clearer reporting standards for execution realism, reproducibility, and evaluation comparability.

title: PhysAgent: Automating Physics-Based 4D Synthesis via Trajectory-Grounded Multi-Agent Feedback
summary: Achieving fully automated, physically plausible 3D motion synthesis is a core objective in graphics and generative AI. However, configuring complex environmental force fields still relies entirely on manual expert intervention, creating a severe bottleneck for large-scale simulation data generation. Existing automated methods primarily focus on material optimization and exhibit severe modality gaps and technical flaws when applied to the vastly more complex force field optimization space: naive Large Language Models (LLMs) lack underlying simulation feedback, causing severe physical inaccuracies, while traditional Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) suffers from sluggish gradients, local optima entrapment, and a mathematical inability to dynamically switch discrete force fields. To address this, we propose PhysAgent, the first simulator-in-the-loop multi-agent framework that leverages multimodal inputs for automated, physically grounded 4D synthesis. By decoupling intrinsic materials from extrinsic dynamics, PhysAgent utilizes a Semantic Agent equipped with an externalized Force Field Skill module to master simulation rules and generate valid initializations. Subsequently, the Refine Agents, driven by Trajectory-Grounded Multi-Agent Feedback, leverage vision foundation models to extract dense point trajectories from rendered frames. By converting these explicit motion trajectories into structured textual descriptors, the agent harnesses LLM commonsense reasoning to execute zero-shot macroscopic leaps, effectively escaping local optima and dynamically switching discrete force fields. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PhysAgent rapidly generates stable, diverse physical scenes from arbitrary multimodal prompts, significantly outperforming existing baselines in both generation diversity and physical accuracy.

AI.tldr: PhysAgent is the first simulator-in-the-loop multi-agent framework for automated, physically grounded 4D motion synthesis. It decouples intrinsic materials from extrinsic dynamics using a Semantic Agent with force field skills and Refine Agents with trajectory-grounded feedback, enabling zero-shot macroscopic leaps and dynamic force field switching. It significantly outperforms baselines in diversity and physical accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current 3D motion synthesis relies on manual expert intervention to configure complex environmental force fields, creating a bottleneck for large-scale simulation data generation. Existing automated methods (LLMs without simulation feedback, SDS with sluggish gradients and local optima) have severe modality gaps and technical flaws when applied to force field optimization.
AI.method: PhysAgent is a multi-agent framework with: (1) a Semantic Agent with an externalized Force Field Skill module to master simulation rules and generate valid initializations; (2) Refine Agents driven by Trajectory-Grounded Multi-Agent Feedback, using vision foundation models to extract dense point trajectories and convert them into structured textual descriptors for LLM commonsense reasoning, enabling zero-shot macroscopic leaps and dynamic discrete force field switching.
AI.result: PhysAgent rapidly generates stable, diverse physical scenes from arbitrary multimodal prompts, significantly outperforming existing baselines in both generation diversity and physical accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Automated, physically plausible 4D synthesis is achievable via a simulator-in-the-loop multi-agent framework that decouples intrinsic/extrinsic physics and leverages trajectory-grounded LLM reasoning, overcoming limitations of both naive LLMs and SDS-based approaches.

title: Ablation-Reversible Heads Don't Transfer: A Stress Test for Mechanistic Role Claims in Transformers
summary: In mechanistic interpretability, attention heads are commonly elevated to role claims (e.g., "this head represents addition") when they are necessary for a behavior, encode it linearly, and recover that behavior when restored after ablation. We show this evidence is insufficient: across three 7-8B instruction-tuned models and five computation families, heads passing all three checks routinely fail to transfer the computation when their activations are patched into a different prompt under matched controls. We introduce KID (Knowing / Intent / Doing), a role-assignment lens for attention heads, and pair it with a three-stage pipeline: capability-selective screening (CSS), singular value decomposition (SVD), and activation transduction under matched controls. Our results document a preliminary role taxonomy (including prompt-trajectory stabilizers, answer-side logit-bias heads, and soft computation-pattern carriers) and show that the same-answer control (a transduction target sharing the answer string but not the requested computation) is an underused check that exposes broad state transfer masquerading as semantic specificity.

AI.tldr: Standard evidence for attributing specific computational roles to attention heads (necessity, linear encoding, recovery after ablation) is insufficient. Heads passing all three checks routinely fail to transfer their computation when activations are patched into different prompts. The paper introduces KID (Knowing/Intent/Doing) role-assignment lens and a three-stage pipeline (CSS, SVD, activation transduction under matched controls), resulting in a preliminary role taxonomy and highlighting the same-answer control as an underused check that exposes state transfer masquerading as semantic specificity.
AI.motivation: Current methods for assigning roles to attention heads in mechanistic interpretability rely on three checks (necessity, linear encoding, recovery after ablation), but these are insufficient for proving that a head truly represents a specific computation.
AI.method: KID (Knowing/Intent/Doing) role-assignment lens paired with a three-stage pipeline: capability-selective screening (CSS), singular value decomposition (SVD), and activation transduction under matched controls.
AI.result: Heads passing standard checks routinely fail to transfer computation via activation patching under matched controls. A preliminary role taxonomy is documented, and same-answer control is identified as an underused check that reveals state transfer masquerading as semantic specificity.
AI.conclusion: Standard evidence for attention head role claims is insufficient; the KID framework and same-answer control provide more rigorous attribution methods.

title: Real-Time and Accurate Collision-Free Teleoperation via Differentiable Constraint-Based Trajectory Planning
summary: In teleoperation, the human operator typically controls only the end-effector pose, which often leads to self-collisions of the manipulator and collisions with environmental obstacles, since joints and links are not controlled individually. A common strategy to mitigate this issue is to enhance the operator's input using optimal-control-based trajectory planning. As derivative-based solvers require differentiable constraints, existing approaches either approximate robots and obstacles with spheres, reducing geometric accuracy, or approximate derivatives, degrading convergence and increasing computation times. We address these limitations by adapting a recent formulation of differentiable collision-avoidance constraints, based on duality in convex optimization, to the teleoperation setting. The robot is approximated with capsules and the environment with polytopes. We compare the resulting trajectory planning method against state-of-the-art techniques in simulation with varying numbers of obstacles and evaluate it on a UR5e manipulator in a real-world teleoperation test. Results show that our approach achieves lower computation times while enabling more accurate obstacle modeling, leading to smoother and collision-free end-effector teleoperation.

AI.tldr: A differentiable collision-avoidance method using convex-optimization-based constraints enables faster, smoother, and collision-free teleoperation with more accurate capsule-polytope robot/environment modeling compared to sphere-based approximations.
AI.motivation: In teleoperation, controlling only the end-effector pose causes self-collisions and collisions with obstacles. Existing optimal-control-based solutions use sphere approximations (reducing geometric accuracy) or approximate derivatives (degrading convergence and increasing computation time).
AI.method: Adapts differentiable collision-avoidance constraints based on duality in convex optimization; represents robot with capsules and environment with polytopes; integrates these into optimal-control-based trajectory planning for teleoperation.
AI.result: Lower computation times, more accurate obstacle modeling, smoother and collision-free end-effector teleoperation compared to state-of-the-art methods in simulation (varying obstacle counts) and on a real UR5e manipulator.
AI.conclusion: The proposed differentiable collision-avoidance formulation using capsule-polytope representations achieves superior geometric accuracy and computational efficiency over sphere-based or derivative-approximation approaches in teleoperation.

title: Revisiting the shutdown problem
summary: A key premise in leading arguments for existential risk from artificial intelligence is that malfunctioning artificial agents could not be easily shut down. This motivates the catastrophic shutdown problem of ensuring that agents can be shut down before they cause an existential catastrophe. A range of arguments and theorems are offered to suggest that solving the catastrophic shutdown problem is difficult, bolstering arguments for existential risk and motivating a search for solutions to the catastrophic shutdown problem. This paper argues for two conclusions. First, existing arguments do not establish the difficulty of solving the catastrophic shutdown problem. Second, concern for the catastrophic shutdown problem has led to technical solutions that impose a high safety tax on model performance.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques existing arguments about the catastrophic shutdown problem in AI safety, arguing they don't prove its difficulty and that proposed solutions impose a high safety tax on model performance.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses claims that malfunctioning AI agents cannot be easily shut down, which underpins existential risk arguments. It aims to challenge these claims and highlight the costs of proposed solutions.
AI.method: The paper provides a critical analysis of existing arguments and theorems regarding the catastrophic shutdown problem, and evaluates technical solutions proposed to address it.
AI.result: Existing arguments do not convincingly establish the difficulty of solving the catastrophic shutdown problem, and current technical solutions impose a significant safety tax on model performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the catastrophic shutdown problem may be more tractable than previously argued, and that the pursuit of solutions should be balanced against performance costs.

title: IR-SIM: A Lightweight Skill-Native Simulator for Navigation, Learning, and Benchmarking
summary: Simulation plays a key role in automated robotics research supported by large language models (LLMs). However, existing simulators often require custom code or complex interfaces, creating a barrier to rapid prototyping and automated algorithm development. To this end, we propose the Intelligent Robot Simulator (IR-SIM), a lightweight skill-native navigation simulator designed for rapid scenario construction, benchmarking, and robot learning. In IR-SIM, scenarios are entirely defined by YAML configuration files that specify mobile robot kinematics, geometric collision checking, LiDAR sensing, visualization, and behavior modules. This design makes robotic simulation fully describable and reproducible, allowing scenarios to be generated and modified from text prompts through the proposed IR-SIM agent skills. The resulting scenarios can be used for automated benchmarking of navigation algorithms and for automated generation of training data for learning methods. Furthermore, IR-SIM provides bridges to high fidelity simulators and real world deployment, allowing users to validate their algorithms in more realistic settings after prototyping without extra coding. The experiments showcase the convenience and versatility of IR-SIM in multiple tasks: constructing navigation scenarios from natural language, training a collision avoidance policy, benchmarking social navigation policies, and bridging to high fidelity simulators and real world deployment. The project website is available at https://github.com/hanruihua/ir-sim.

AI.tldr: IR-SIM is a lightweight, YAML-configurable robot navigation simulator that enables rapid scenario construction, benchmarking, and robot learning, with LLM-based text-to-scenario generation and seamless bridges to high-fidelity simulators and real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing simulators require custom code or complex interfaces, creating barriers to rapid prototyping and automated algorithm development in LLM-supported robotics research.
AI.method: IR-SIM defines scenarios entirely through YAML configuration files specifying kinematics, collision checking, LiDAR, visualization, and behavior modules; it also provides IR-SIM agent skills for text-prompt-based scenario generation/modification via LLMs.
AI.result: Demonstrated convenience and versatility in constructing navigation scenarios from natural language, training collision avoidance policies, benchmarking social navigation policies, and bridging to high-fidelity simulators and real-world deployment.
AI.conclusion: IR-SIM enables fully describable and reproducible robotic simulation, facilitating automated benchmarking and data generation while supporting seamless transition from prototyping to realistic validation without extra coding.

title: To Nuke or Not to Nuke: LLMs' (Missing) Ethical Reasoning and Actions in a High-Stakes Decision-Making Simulation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as long-horizon agents with decision-making capacities. While LLMs can show ethical competence on dilemmas such as trolley problems, this competence may not translate to complex, agentic scenarios. We study this gap in Civilization V, a multiplayer game with a complex decision-making landscape including economy, diplomacy, technology, and military strategy. Starting from 130 high-tension LLM self-play episodes, in which an LLM player spontaneously escalated nuclear authorization, we replay them across 13 models with three prompt interventions: an ethical prompt naming nuclear harm, removal of the previous model's decision-making rationale, and high-stakes framing emphasizing real-world impacts. No interventions nor their combinations reliably eliminate emergent escalation. We identify three failure pathways: ethical reasoning that fails to surface without prompting, fails to appear even when prompted, or surfaces but fails to take effect when strategic counter-factors dominate. Evaluations of agentic models, therefore, must test whether ethical reasoning is spontaneously invoked and behaviorally effective in complex decision-making contexts, beyond whether it can be elicited in isolation.

AI.tldr: LLMs deployed as long-horizon agents in Civilization V spontaneously escalate to nuclear war. Ethical prompts, removing rationale, and high-stakes framing fail to reliably prevent escalation. Three failure pathways identified: ethical reasoning fails to surface, fails to appear when prompted, or surfaces but is overridden by strategic factors.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs' ethical competence on isolated dilemmas (e.g., trolley problems) transfers to complex, agentic decision-making contexts where strategic and multi-factor trade-offs are present.
AI.method: Analyzed 130 high-tension LLM self-play episodes from Civilization V where nuclear escalation spontaneously occurred. Replayed them across 13 models with three prompt interventions: (1) ethical prompt naming nuclear harm, (2) removal of previous decision-making rationale, and (3) high-stakes framing emphasizing real-world impacts.
AI.result: No single intervention nor any combination reliably eliminated emergent nuclear escalation. Identified three failure pathways: ethical reasoning fails to surface without prompting, fails to appear even when prompted, or surfaces but is behaviorally overridden by strategic counter-factors.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of agentic LLMs must test whether ethical reasoning is spontaneously invoked and behaviorally effective in complex decision-making contexts, not merely whether it can be elicited in isolation.

title: Dream-Tac: A Unified Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
summary: World action models inherit the predictive capability of world models, enabling action generation to be guided by anticipated future observations. However, they rely primarily on vision and often fail in contact-rich manipulation, where critical cues arise from physical interaction. In this paper, we propose Dream-Tac, a unified Tactile-World Action Model that jointly models actions, future visual observations, and tactile dynamics. Specifically, Dream-Tac introduces (i) contact-gated visuotactile fusion to selectively integrate tactile signals and (ii) a contact-aware attention bias to better regulate cross-modal interactions during manipulation. To support real-time deployment, we further design a dual-level acceleration strategy, reformulating the contact-aware bias to preserve the fused attention path during training and introducing cache-based diffusion acceleration at inference, achieving up to 2.9$\times$ faster training and 1.8$\times$ faster inference. Across six contact-rich manipulation tasks, Dream-Tac improves action accuracy by 31.7\% on average, demonstrating the effectiveness of unified visuotactile world modeling.Code is available at https://github.com/LYFCLOUDFAN/Dream-Tac.

AI.tldr: Dream-Tac is a unified Tactile-World Action Model that integrates vision and tactile feedback for contact-rich manipulation, achieving 31.7% better action accuracy through contact-gated visuotactile fusion and dual-level acceleration (2.9× faster training, 1.8× faster inference).
AI.motivation: Existing world action models rely primarily on vision and fail in contact-rich manipulation because critical cues arise from physical interaction (tactile feedback) rather than visual observation alone.
AI.method: Dream-Tac introduces (i) contact-gated visuotactile fusion to selectively integrate tactile signals, (ii) contact-aware attention bias for regulating cross-modal interactions, and (iii) a dual-level acceleration strategy including reformulated contact-aware bias for training and cache-based diffusion acceleration for inference.
AI.result: Achieves 31.7% average improvement in action accuracy across six contact-rich manipulation tasks, with 2.9× faster training and 1.8× faster inference.
AI.conclusion: Unified visuotactile world modeling effectively improves action generation in contact-rich manipulation, demonstrating the importance of jointly modeling actions, visual observations, and tactile dynamics.

title: Curation of a Cardiology Interface Terminology for Highlighting Electronic Health Records using Machine Learning
summary: Electronic health record (EHR) notes are dense medical documents containing large amounts of information, often filled with complex medical jargon. Highlighting all details in EHRs helps reduce the likelihood of missing crucial information by drawing attention to key content. This study proposes the design of a Cardiology Interface Terminology (CIT) to accurately highlight all details in EHR notes of cardiology patients. We introduce an innovative Machine Learning (ML) technique for the design of CIT. The ML technique requires training data. Manual preparation of such training data is time-consuming and expensive. The process of the CIT design includes three phases. In the first two phases, we innovatively derive a training data CIT to be used by the third phase, ML technique. We start by designing an initial CIT, composed of several components: the cardiology-related sub-hierarchies of SNOMED, other SNOMED concepts mined from EHRs of build set, and necessary components of terms e.g., medical abbreviations and medications. Utilizing an iterative process, fine-grained phrases containing initial CIT concepts are extracted from build set as CIT concept candidates. The candidate concepts are semi-automatically reviewed before being added to CIT, yielding the training data CIT, TCIT. In the third phase, a ML model is trained with TCIT to identify candidates fitting to be concepts in the CIT. This model is used to extract further concepts from build set, yielding the final CIT. The final CIT is then used to highlight the test set and evaluate the extent to which it captures details in an unseen EHR dataset. For this purpose, four evaluation metrics, coverage, breadth, completeness, and conciseness are used. The highlighted test set has a coverage of 74.21%, with a breadth of 1.68. For 20 random notes in test set, the average completeness is 98.2% and average conciseness is 84.2%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Cardiology Interface Terminology (CIT) using a three-phase ML approach with semi-automatically generated training data to highlight key details in EHR notes, achieving 74.21% coverage, 1.68 breadth, 98.2% completeness, and 84.2% conciseness on test data.
AI.motivation: EHR notes contain dense medical information with complex jargon; highlighting all details helps reduce the likelihood of missing crucial clinical information by drawing attention to key content.
AI.method: Three-phase CIT design: (1) Initial CIT using SNOMED cardiology sub-hierarchies, mined concepts, and medical terms; (2) Iterative extraction and semi-automatic review of fine-grained candidate phrases to build training data (TCIT); (3) ML model trained on TCIT to extract additional concepts, yielding the final CIT for highlighting.
AI.result: Test set coverage of 74.21%, breadth of 1.68. For 20 random notes: average completeness 98.2%, average conciseness 84.2%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ML-based CIT design effectively highlights cardiology EHR details with high completeness and conciseness, reducing manual annotation effort through semi-automated training data generation.

title: Safe, Fluent and Acceptable Motion Generation and Execution for Human--Robot Interaction in Manufacturing Environments
summary: Robots operating in human environments must not only ensure physical safety but also exhibit behaviors that are understandable, fluent, and acceptable to human partners. This paper investigates motion generation strategies that combine safety guarantees with interaction quality considerations, such as motion smoothness and human comfort. While the design of robots capable of ensuring safety in shared human-robot environments has enabled closer and more advanced forms of interaction, these new proximity-based tasks require moving beyond purely technical considerations. In particular, robot behavior must also be addressed from psycho-cognitive and social perspectives. In this context, we argue for the relevance of integrating social-aware motion control into robotic systems. First, we identify the motion parameters that influence human perception and operator experience. Then, we implement a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework that generates four distinct socially-informed robot behaviors. Finally, we conduct a user study to evaluate and validate these behaviors and assess their social impact on non-expert participants. The results demonstrate that variations in robot behavior significantly affect the perceived social acceptability of the system. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating human-centered considerations into motion generation strategies for robots operating in shared environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes integrating social-aware motion control into robotic systems to make robot behaviors not only safe but also socially acceptable. It identifies key motion parameters affecting human perception, implements an MPC framework generating four socially-informed behaviors, and validates through a user study that behavior variations significantly impact perceived social acceptability.
AI.motivation: Robots in human environments need behaviors that are understandable, fluent, and acceptable beyond just physical safety. Proximity-based tasks require psycho-cognitive and social perspectives, not purely technical safety guarantees.
AI.method: (1) Identify motion parameters influencing human perception; (2) Implement a Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework generating four distinct socially-informed robot behaviors; (3) Conduct a user study with non-expert participants to evaluate social impact.
AI.result: Variations in robot behavior significantly affect perceived social acceptability of the system.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating human-centered considerations into motion generation strategies is important for robots operating in shared environments.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Injection of LTLf Constraints in Autoregressive Reinforcement Learning Policies
comment: Accepted at the Joint Workshop on Statistics and Knowledge Integration for Logic, Learning, Ethical Decisions, and LLMs (SKILLED-LLMs 2026), co-located with KR 2026 and FLoC 2026, Lisbon, Portugal
summary: In this work we study offline reinforcement learning (RL) under temporally extended task constraints expressed in Linear Temporal Logic over finite traces (LTLf). Recently, transformer-based approaches such as Trajectory Transformers and Decision Transformers have been adopted to address RL as a sequence modeling problem. However, these methods optimize purely for reward and do not account for high-level temporal requirements. Here, we introduce a neurosymbolic framework that injects LTLf background knowledge into such transformer-based RL policies. Our approach compiles LTLf formulas into deterministic finite automata (DFAs) and integrates them into the learning process through a differentiable representation and a logic-based loss function. In particular, we derive differentiable satisfaction signals from DFA progression and use them as a regularization term during training. The resulting method is architecture-agnostic across different models. We evaluate the proposed framework on navigation environments with specification suites covering combinations of safety and reachability temporal properties. Experimental results show that incorporating background knowledge not only improves constraint satisfaction, but also maintains competitive return compared to vanilla baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neurosymbolic framework combining LTLf temporal constraints with transformer-based offline RL models. It compiles LTLf specifications into DFAs, derives differentiable satisfaction signals via DFA progression, and uses a logic-based regularization loss during training. Experiments on navigation tasks show improved constraint satisfaction while maintaining competitive returns.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based RL approaches (e.g., Decision Transformers) optimize purely for reward and fail to account for high-level temporal requirements expressed in formal specifications like LTLf.
AI.method: Compiles LTLf formulas into DFAs; derives differentiable satisfaction signals from DFA progression; integrates them as a logic-based regularization loss into transformer-based RL training; architecture-agnostic across different models.
AI.result: The proposed framework improves constraint satisfaction on safety and reachability temporal properties in navigation environments while maintaining competitive reward returns compared to vanilla baselines.
AI.conclusion: Injecting LTLf background knowledge via differentiable DFA progression and logic-based regularization enhances transformer-based offline RL policies' ability to satisfy temporally extended constraints without sacrificing reward performance.

title: Guided Discovery of New Behaviors using Diffusion Policies
summary: Diffusion models have become a powerful tool for generative modeling in robotics, with diffusion policies excelling at modeling multimodal action-trajectory distributions. However, when demonstrations are limited, standard sampling often reproduces dominant behaviors while neglecting valid but rare modes, limiting the discovery of novel solutions. Existing approaches, such as guidance methods or combining reinforcement learning with diffusion, either push samples into infeasible regions or struggle to escape local minima, failing to systematically uncover diverse behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose a framework that combines Feynman-Kac correctors with a novel guiding potential that systematically guides diffusion policy samples towards promising yet underrepresented samples. These trajectories are refined using sampling-based trajectory optimization and reincorporated into the training set to retrain the diffusion policy. Our method effectively mines and repairs novel trajectories, enabling the systematic discovery of diverse and executable behaviors. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across a range of manipulation environments, consistently discovering new behaviors.

AI.tldr: A framework combining Feynman-Kac correctors with guiding potentials to systematically discover diverse, underrepresented behaviors from limited demonstrations in diffusion policies for robotics.
AI.motivation: Standard diffusion policy sampling from limited demonstrations over-represents dominant behaviors and neglects rare modes, while existing methods (guidance, RL+diffusion) either produce infeasible samples or get stuck in local minima, failing to systematically uncover diverse solutions.
AI.method: Combines Feynman-Kac correctors with a novel guiding potential to steer diffusion policy samples toward promising but underrepresented trajectories; refines them via sampling-based trajectory optimization; then reincorporates repaired trajectories into training set for retraining the diffusion policy.
AI.result: Demonstrates consistent discovery of new, diverse, and executable behaviors across multiple manipulation environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively mines and repairs novel trajectories, enabling systematic discovery of diverse behaviors from limited demonstrations in robotic manipulation tasks.

title: Integrating Deep Learning Demand Forecasting with Multi-Objective Optimization for Circular Coffee Supply Chains: A Data-Driven Framework for Cost, Emissions, and Freshness Management
summary:
The coffee supply chain is one of the most complex agri-food networks, marked by geographically dispersed production, multi-tier coordination, and high sensitivity to quality and freshness. While sustainability and digitalization have gained attention, demand forecasting, optimization, and traceability are often treated separately. This study presents a two-phase integrated framework. First, a hybrid CNN-LSTM model is used for demand forecasting. On the public Coffee Chain Sales dataset with chronological 70/15/15 splitting, the model achieves MAE of 22.87 and R^2 of 0.90, outperforming the best deep learning benchmark by ~12% and classical methods by over 30%. In the second phase, the forecasted demand feeds a tri-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that jointly minimizes cost, minimizes carbon emissions, and maximizes product freshness in a multi-period, multimodal, closed-loop supply chain with circular recovery. Freshness is modeled via exponential decay based on inventory age. Using the epsilon-constraint method, 25 Pareto solutions are obtained. Sensitivity and policy analyses show that balanced sustainability policies can reduce emissions by 22.4% with only a 9.9% cost increase while maintaining near-optimal freshness.
  Keywords: Coffee supply chain; Deep learning; Demand forecasting; Multi-objective optimization; Circular economy; CNN-LSTM; Mixed-integer linear programming.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-phase integrated framework for coffee supply chain management: a hybrid CNN-LSTM model for demand forecasting (achieving MAE of 22.87 and R² of 0.90, outperforming baselines by 12-30%), followed by a tri-objective MILP model that jointly optimizes cost, carbon emissions, and product freshness in a closed-loop supply chain. Policy analysis shows balanced sustainability policies can reduce emissions by 22.4% with only a 9.9% cost increase.
AI.motivation: The coffee supply chain is highly complex due to geographically dispersed production, multi-tier coordination, and freshness sensitivity. Demand forecasting, optimization, and traceability are often treated separately in existing research, motivating the need for an integrated framework.
AI.method: A two-phase framework: (1) A hybrid CNN-LSTM deep learning model for demand forecasting on the Coffee Chain Sales dataset with chronological 70/15/15 train/validation/test split. (2) A tri-objective mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model minimizing cost, carbon emissions, and maximizing freshness (modeled via exponential decay based on inventory age) in a multi-period, multimodal, closed-loop supply chain. Pareto solutions are generated via the epsilon-constraint method.
AI.result: The CNN-LSTM model achieves MAE of 22.87 and R² of 0.90, outperforming the best deep learning benchmark by ~12% and classical methods by over 30%. The MILP optimization yields 25 Pareto solutions. Sensitivity and policy analyses show balanced sustainability policies can reduce emissions by 22.4% with only a 9.9% cost increase while maintaining near-optimal freshness.
AI.conclusion: The integrated forecasting-optimization framework effectively addresses the coffee supply chain's complexity, demonstrating that balanced sustainability policies can achieve significant emission reductions with modest cost increases, supporting circular economy principles in agri-food networks.

title: RGB-S: Image-Aligned Tactile Saliency for Robust Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Effective visuo-tactile integration is critical for robotic dexterous manipulation, especially when visual observations are unreliable or occluded. However, robustly aligning sparse, heterogeneous tactile measurements with dense visual representations remains a fundamental challenge. Most existing approaches require policies to learn cross-modal correspondences implicitly from limited demonstrations, without leveraging geometric priors. As a result, they are often data-inefficient and generalize poorly when visual observations are degraded. To address this limitation, we propose a framework that explicitly grounds physical contacts in the image domain. Using robot forward kinematics and camera calibration, we project tactile sensor locations directly onto the RGB image plane. We then render force-modulated Gaussian saliency maps to model spatial uncertainty arising from kinematic and calibration errors. By integrating these 2D spatial anchors through a zero-initialized conditioning architecture, our method injects physical contact priors into standard visual backbones while preserving pre-trained visual representations. We evaluate our method on six dexterous manipulation tasks in both simulation and the real world under severe visual occlusions. Real-world experiments show that explicit RGB-S grounding in the image domain improves real-world occluded manipulation success rates by $26.7$ percentage points over the strongest implicit visuo-tactile baseline, suggesting its improved spatial reasoning and robustness to occlusion. Project page: touch-as-saliency.github.io

AI.tldr: An explicit visuo-tactile grounding framework that projects tactile sensor locations onto RGB images using kinematic and calibration priors, with force-modulated Gaussian saliency maps, improving dexterous manipulation under occlusion by 26.7 percentage points over implicit baselines.
AI.motivation: Robust visuo-tactile integration is critical for dexterous manipulation under visual occlusion, but existing implicit methods that learn cross-modal correspondences from limited demonstrations are data-inefficient and generalize poorly when visual observations are degraded.
AI.method: Project tactile sensor locations onto RGB image plane using forward kinematics and camera calibration; render force-modulated Gaussian saliency maps to model spatial uncertainty; inject these 2D anchors via zero-initialized conditioning into visual backbones while preserving pre-trained representations.
AI.result: On six dexterous manipulation tasks under severe occlusion, the method improves real-world success rates by 26.7 percentage points over the strongest implicit visuo-tactile baseline.
AI.conclusion: Explicit RGB-S grounding in the image domain improves spatial reasoning and robustness to occlusion, demonstrating significant gains over implicit cross-modal correspondence learning approaches.

title: Benchmarking Open-Ended Multi-Agent Coordination in Language Agents
summary: As language models are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, they must coordinate with others over long horizons in open-ended interactive tasks. Yet existing evaluations rarely test these demands together, instead emphasising single-agent tasks, short interactions, or highly structured multi-agent settings. We introduce $alem$, a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics. Alem embeds procedurally generated coordination tasks, soft specialisation, communication, and controllable coordination difficulty into a long-horizon survival world with exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. We evaluate $13$ modern LLMs zero-shot within homogeneous teams, with trained MARL agents as reference points. Current LLM agents remain far from solving alem, averaging only ~6% normalised return, but their failures are not uniform. On the hardest coordination setting, zero-shot Gemini-3.1-Pro-High approaches MARL agents trained for one billion steps, while GPT-5.4-High achieves strong base-task reward but much lower coordination reward. This contrast shows that individual task competence does not imply coordination competence. Ablations show that communication is the largest contributor to coordination, while memory and reasoning help when used to maintain multi-step plans. Overall, our results identify coordination as a distinct bottleneck for frontier LLM agents, separate from single-agent capabilities. Alem makes this bottleneck measurable and provides a controlled testbed for developing agents that communicate, allocate roles, and execute shared plans. Code is available at https://github.com/alem-world/alem-env.

AI.tldr: Alem is a JAX-based benchmark for open-ended multi-agent coordination built on Craftax-like dynamics, evaluating 13 LLMs in homogeneous teams. Current LLM agents average ~6% normalized return, with coordination identified as a distinct bottleneck separate from single-agent capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations rarely test long-horizon, open-ended multi-agent coordination together, instead emphasizing single-agent tasks, short interactions, or highly structured multi-agent settings.
AI.method: Alem embeds procedurally generated coordination tasks, soft specialisation, communication, and controllable coordination difficulty into a long-horizon survival world with exploration, crafting, trading, and combat. 13 modern LLMs are evaluated zero-shot within homogeneous teams, with trained MARL agents as baselines.
