An end-to-end online replay shows the judge-call rate falling (50% to 44%) and judge-domain accuracy rising (71% to 80%), with 0 benign hard-blocks across 45,000 actions.

AI.tldr: AgentTrust v2 is a dual-store trust layer for AI agent actions that uses an LLM judge to handle semantic threats (which rule-based systems cannot address) and distills deterministic rules for lexical threats, achieving near-zero false blocks and self-improving accuracy over time.
AI.motivation: AI agents execute consequential actions (shell commands, cloud operations, tool calls) but existing trust layers rely on static rules that fail for semantic (intent-dependent) threats where benign and malicious actions share the same surface form.
AI.method: A dual-store system: (1) an LLM judge handles semantic threats with self-learning from a growing corpus; (2) deterministic rules are distilled from the judge for lexical (fixed-signature) threats; (3) a guarded RAG memory with a corroboration guard prevents surface-twin failures in verdict caches.
AI.result: Rule packs capped at ~56% accuracy and 0pp gain on semantic categories; LLM judge nearly doubles accuracy to 83.6-85.2% with near-zero false blocks; guarded RAG lifts semantic accuracy +13pp (70 to 84); online replay shows judge-call rate dropping 50%→44% and accuracy rising 71%→80% with 0 benign hard-blocks across 45K actions.
AI.conclusion: A trust layer can self-evolve from its own decision stream — cheaper on lexical class via distilled rules, smarter on semantic class via guarded precedent — without ever hard-blocking a benign action.

title: MotionWAM: Towards Foundation World Action Models for Real-Time Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) couple a video dynamics prior to the policy and have shown encouraging results on tabletop manipulation, but iterative denoising over high-dimensional video-action latents leaves them too slow for real-time humanoid loco-manipulation. The problem is compounded by the dominant hierarchical paradigm, in which a high-level manipulation policy controls only the upper body while a low-level controller tracks coarse base commands -- placing upper and lower body in inconsistent action spaces and reducing the legs to balance-preserving locomotion. We present MotionWAM, a real-time WAM that drives autonomous humanoid loco-manipulation from a single egocentric camera by conditioning the policy on the intermediate denoising features of a video world model. MotionWAM replaces the upper-lower split with a unified motion latent and predicts whole-body motion tokens that jointly cover locomotion, torso motion, height regulation, foot interaction, and hand manipulation in a single action space. A three-stage learning framework progressively adapts the video world model to egocentric visual dynamics and to the target humanoid embodiment. On nine real-world Unitree G1 tasks, MotionWAM runs in real time, substantially outperforms Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines fine-tuned on the same demonstrations by over 30% in overall success rate, and executes task-driven foot interaction that decoupled upper-lower policies cannot reach. Our results suggest that video-pretrained WAMs can be lifted from tabletop manipulation to coordinated, human-like whole-body humanoid control.

AI.tldr: MotionWAM is a real-time World Action Model for humanoid loco-manipulation that replaces hierarchical upper/lower body control with a unified whole-body motion latent, achieving over 30% higher success rates than VLA baselines on real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing WAMs are too slow for real-time humanoid loco-manipulation due to iterative denoising over high-dimensional video-action latents, and the dominant hierarchical paradigm separates upper and lower body into inconsistent action spaces, reducing legs to balance-preserving locomotion rather than coordinated whole-body tasks.
AI.method: MotionWAM conditions the policy on intermediate denoising features of a video world model, replaces the upper-lower split with a unified motion latent predicting whole-body motion tokens (locomotion, torso, height, foot interaction, manipulation) in a single action space, and uses a three-stage learning framework to adapt the video world model to egocentric visual dynamics and the target humanoid embodiment.
AI.result: On nine real-world Unitree G1 tasks, MotionWAM runs in real time, outperforms VLA baselines fine-tuned on the same demonstrations by over 30% in overall success rate, and executes task-driven foot interaction that decoupled upper-lower policies cannot achieve.
AI.conclusion: Video-pretrained WAMs can be lifted from tabletop manipulation to coordinated, human-like whole-body humanoid control.

title: PAEC: Position-Aware Entropy Calibration for LLM Reasoning in RLVR
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model reasoning but often suffers from rapid policy-entropy collapse, where the policy prematurely concentrates on narrow high-probability reasoning paths. While global entropy regularization can encourage exploration, uniformly increasing entropy across all token positions is inefficient for long reasoning trajectories, where many tokens are not decision-relevant. We propose Position-Aware Entropy Calibration (PAEC), a token-level entropy-management framework that constructs a soft mask from local top-p entropy and top-two candidate competition, and applies an anchor-based lower-bound penalty to prevent selected-position entropy collapse. Experiments on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that PAEC improves macro-average majority-vote performance over strong RLVR baselines, with clear gains on AIME-style tasks. Our results suggest that entropy management in reasoning RL should be formulated as selective exploration allocation over decision-sensitive positions rather than uniform randomness injection.

AI.tldr: PAEC is a token-level entropy management framework that prevents policy-entropy collapse in RLVR by selectively applying entropy regularization only to decision-relevant positions, improving reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RLVR improves LLM reasoning but suffers from rapid policy-entropy collapse, where the policy prematurely concentrates on narrow reasoning paths. Global entropy regularization is inefficient for long reasoning trajectories because many tokens are not decision-relevant.
AI.method: PAEC constructs a soft mask from local top-p entropy and top-two candidate competition, then applies an anchor-based lower-bound penalty to prevent entropy collapse at selected (decision-sensitive) positions.
AI.result: PAEC improves macro-average majority-vote performance over strong RLVR baselines on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with clear gains on AIME-style tasks.
AI.conclusion: Entropy management in reasoning RL should be formulated as selective exploration allocation over decision-sensitive positions rather than uniform randomness injection.

title: Self-Paced Curriculum Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Superbike Racing in Simulation
comment: Presented at the "1st Workshop on Generalization in Autonomous Driving: Paradigms, Practice, and Public Road Demonstrations" at ICRA 2026, Vienna. Oral+poster presentation
summary: Autonomous Racing has seen remarkable progress through deep Reinforcement Learning (RL), primarily for four-wheeled vehicles. However, motorbikes introduce substantially greater complexity due to the need to manage balance and lean angle, in addition to more reactive steering and throttle control, and a smaller weight. In this work, we present a framework for training an autonomous agent to race a superbike in VRider SBK, a physics-accurate Unity-based motorbike simulator. Our approach integrates Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with Self-Paced curriculum Deep reinforcement Learning (SPDL), which dynamically generates progressively more challenging tasks based on the agent's performance, without requiring manual curriculum design. The agent's state space comprises proprioceptive features extended with lean-angle history, along with global track features via course points. The reward signal is shaped to encourage progress along the track while penalizing instability-inducing behaviors specific to two-wheeled dynamics. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate that SPDL outperforms SAC alone in training efficiency, lap time, and driving stability across multiple tracks and motorbike models, establishing a first baseline for RL-based autonomous motorbike racing.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a framework for autonomous superbike racing using Soft Actor-Critic combined with Self-Paced curriculum Deep reinforcement Learning (SPDL) in a physics-accurate Unity simulator, showing that SPDL outperforms SAC alone in training efficiency, lap time, and stability across multiple tracks and bike models.
AI.motivation: Autonomous racing has advanced for four-wheeled vehicles via deep RL, but motorbikes are significantly more challenging due to the need to manage balance, lean angle, reactive steering/throttle control, and smaller weight — yet no prior RL-based solution existed for autonomous motorbike racing.
AI.method: The framework integrates Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) with Self-Paced curriculum Deep reinforcement Learning (SPDL) to dynamically generate progressively harder tasks based on agent performance without manual curriculum design. State space uses proprioceptive features with lean-angle history and global track features via course points. Reward shaping encourages track progress while penalizing instability-inducing behaviors specific to two-wheeled dynamics.
AI.result: SPDL outperforms SAC alone in training efficiency, lap time, and driving stability across multiple tracks and motorbike models, establishing a first baseline for RL-based autonomous motorbike racing.
AI.conclusion: SPDL is an effective curriculum learning approach for training autonomous motorbike agents in complex two-wheeled dynamics, achieving superior performance over standard SAC without requiring manual curriculum design.

title: Quantitative Promise Theory: Intentionality and Inference in Autonomous Agents
summary: I discuss some quantitative representations of Promise Theory for processes involving autonomous agents. Agent models are common in software systems, machine learning, and biology, for example, but may also apply to physics and other forms of engineering. I describe how Bayesian probability and information theoretic optimization, including Active Inference, may be incorporated with promise semantics -- as well as how Promise Theory supplements solutions, helping to avoid probability's pitfalls, which include non-local coordination, calibrating, and normalizing probabilistic computations. The role of boundary conditions in constraining allowed states and selecting decision thresholds is a form of promise, and agent alignment provides a scalable definition of intent. Autonomous agents may congeal into swarms with superagent characteristics by trying to minimize their information, despite uncertainty that works to maximize it. The use of Promise Theory involves some research challenges as well as stylistic preferences.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates Promise Theory with Bayesian probability, information theory, and Active Inference for modeling autonomous agents, showing how promise semantics can avoid pitfalls of probabilistic coordination while enabling scalable agent alignment and swarm formation.
AI.motivation: To develop quantitative representations of Promise Theory for autonomous agents that can incorporate probabilistic methods (Bayesian inference, Active Inference) while overcoming limitations like non-local coordination, calibration, and normalization issues inherent in purely probabilistic approaches.
AI.method: The author describes how Promise Theory semantics can be integrated with Bayesian probability and information-theoretic optimization (including Active Inference), using boundary conditions as promises to constrain states and select decision thresholds, and leveraging agent alignment as a scalable definition of intent.
AI.result: Promise Theory supplements probabilistic solutions by avoiding non-local coordination, calibration, and normalization pitfalls. Autonomous agents can form swarms with superagent characteristics through information minimization, even under uncertainty that drives maximization. Boundary conditions act as promises that constrain allowed states.
AI.conclusion: Promise Theory offers complementary advantages over purely probabilistic approaches for agent-based modeling, though it presents research challenges and stylistic preferences that require further exploration.

title: Can we stabilize an inverted pendulum with feedback from a time-of-flight camera?
summary: Time-of-flight cameras are popular in robotics for providing direct depth information while being compact, inexpensive, and robust to lighting conditions, but their low spatial resolution and depth noise are widely believed to preclude precise feedback control. In this paper, we show that an inexpensive, low-resolution time-of-flight camera provides sufficient feedback to reliably and precisely balance an inverted pendulum on a cart--a canonical benchmark for fast, unstable dynamics.

AI.tldr: Time-of-flight cameras, despite low resolution and depth noise, can provide sufficient feedback to reliably and precisely balance an inverted pendulum on a cart.
AI.motivation: To challenge the prevailing belief that low-resolution, noisy time-of-flight cameras cannot support precise feedback control for fast, unstable dynamics.
AI.method: Using an inexpensive, low-resolution time-of-flight camera as the sole feedback sensor to balance an inverted pendulum on a cart, a canonical benchmark for fast, unstable dynamics.
AI.result: The low-resolution time-of-flight camera provided sufficient feedback to reliably and precisely balance the inverted pendulum.
AI.conclusion: Inexpensive, low-resolution time-of-flight cameras are viable for precise feedback control in fast, unstable dynamic systems, contradicting common assumptions.

title: Distilling LLM Reasoning into an Interpretable Policy Tree for Human-AI Collaboration
summary: Constructing efficient and reliable policies to assist humans is indispensable for human-AI collaboration. Existing methods mainly follow two lines of work. Most prior work relies on multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to learn black-box policies, which limits interpretability and raises safety concerns. Recent methods query large language models (LLMs) at each decision step, causing slow responses and high inference costs. We propose Collaboration Policy Tree (Co-pi-tree), a closed-loop method that learns an executable policy tree consisting of a partner-behavior prediction tree and an agent-action selection tree. Co-pi-tree constructs a policy by distilling LLM reasoning into policy tree code. It then evaluates the policy through partner interaction, obtains feedback, and uses natural language to summarize the interaction feedback to improve problematic branches. Experiments in Overcooked-AI show that Co-pi-tree improves average reward by 35.4% over the baseline average, while reducing the number of LLM queries by 77.7% and test-time latency by 97.1%. Project page: https://beiwenzhang.github.io/Co-pi-tree/

AI.tldr: Co-pi-tree is a closed-loop method that distills LLM reasoning into policy trees for human-AI collaboration, achieving 35.4% higher rewards while reducing LLM queries by 77.7% and latency by 97.1% in Overcooked-AI.
AI.motivation: Existing human-AI collaboration methods either use black-box MARL policies lacking interpretability and safety, or query LLMs at every decision step causing high latency and cost. There is a need for an efficient, interpretable, and safe policy learning approach.
AI.method: Co-pi-tree constructs a policy tree comprising a partner-behavior prediction tree and an agent-action selection tree. It distills LLM reasoning into executable policy tree code, evaluates through partner interaction, collects feedback, and uses natural language summarization to iteratively improve problematic branches.
AI.result: In Overcooked-AI, Co-pi-tree improves average reward by 35.4% over baseline, reduces LLM queries by 77.7%, and reduces test-time latency by 97.1%.
AI.conclusion: Co-pi-tree effectively combines LLM reasoning distillation with closed-loop feedback for efficient, interpretable human-AI collaboration policies.

title: RPO-PDT: Demonstrating Role-Play-Based Knowledge Adaptation for Student Support Dialogue (Demonstration System)
summary: We present RPO-PDT: a retrieval-grounded, role-play-based dialogue system for adaptive student support in higher education. RPO-PDT is: (1) able to provide institution-specific Personal Development Tutor (PDT) guidance using structured knowledge sources; (2) constrained by explicit persona, boundary, confidentiality, and safety policies; and (3) designed around a reverse-roleplay loop where unresolved interactions are replayed from the student perspective, enabling alternative tutor strategies to be generated and stored as reusable strategy memory. RPO-PDT supports both text-based and Furhat-based embodied interaction for demonstrating grounded, safe, and adaptive student-support dialogue.

AI.tldr: RPO-PDT is a retrieval-grounded, role-play-based dialogue system that provides adaptive, safe, and institution-specific student support in higher education through reverse-roleplay loops and embodied interaction capabilities.
AI.motivation: To address the need for adaptive, safe, and institution-specific personal development tutoring in higher education, where student support must be grounded in structured knowledge and constrained by ethical and safety policies.
AI.method: The system integrates retrieval-grounded generation from structured knowledge sources, role-play-based dialogue constrained by persona and safety policies, and a reverse-roleplay loop that replays unresolved interactions from the student perspective to generate alternative tutor strategies stored as reusable strategy memory.
AI.result: The system supports both text-based and Furhat-based embodied interaction, demonstrating grounded, safe, and adaptive student-support dialogue.
AI.conclusion: RPO-PDT offers a novel approach to adaptive student support by combining retrieval grounding, role-play, and reverse-roleplay loops with reusable strategy memory, enabling safe and institution-specific PDT guidance across multiple interaction modalities.

title: InA-Probe: Instruction-Aware Active Probing for Time Series Forecasting with LLMs
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated impressive potential for time series forecasting. However, existing methods predominantly rely on passive modality alignment or static task reprogramming, which often fail to capture fine-grained, non-stationary temporal patterns or to adapt to nuanced task intents. In this paper, we propose Instruction-aware Active Probing (InA-Probe), which shifts the paradigm from passive alignment toward an active, instruction-driven probing mechanism. Specifically, we design a Multi-Level Instruction Injection mechanism that enriches the model with both global task objectives and fine-grained, patch-level semantic priors. Building on this, an Adaptive Query Generation module produces sample-specific probes that are dynamically modulated by the temporal context. These probes are then refined through a dual-stage attention process: they first internalize task-specific intents via Instruction-Aware Self-Attention, and subsequently interrogate the projected temporal representations through Temporal Cross-Attention to extract salient patterns. Comprehensive experiments on seven real-world benchmarks show that InA-Probe consistently outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning and LLM-based baselines, excelling in both one-for-all generalization and zero-shot transfer while reducing forecasting error by up to 37\% in challenging cross-domain scenarios. Ablation studies further confirm that the synergy between adaptive querying and fine-grained instructions is key to unlocking the reasoning power of LLMs for complex time series.

AI.tldr: InA-Probe shifts time series forecasting from passive alignment to active, instruction-driven probing using Multi-Level Instruction Injection, Adaptive Query Generation, and dual-stage attention, achieving SOTA results with up to 37% error reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based time series methods rely on passive modality alignment or static task reprogramming, failing to capture fine-grained non-stationary temporal patterns and adapt to nuanced task intents.
AI.method: (1) Multi-Level Instruction Injection (global task objectives + patch-level semantic priors); (2) Adaptive Query Generation (sample-specific, temporally-modulated probes); (3) Dual-Stage Attention (Instruction-Aware Self-Attention for intent internalization + Temporal Cross-Attention for salient pattern extraction).
AI.result: Outperforms SOTA deep learning and LLM baselines on 7 benchmarks; achieves up to 37% error reduction in cross-domain zero-shot scenarios; excels in one-for-all generalization.
AI.conclusion: The synergy between adaptive querying and fine-grained instructions unlocks LLM reasoning for complex time series; ablation confirms each component's necessity.

title: Back to the Familiar Future: Failure Recovery for VLA Policies via Pre-Imagined Milestone Selection
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can deviate from nominal trajectories during manipulation, even when tasks remain physically feasible. Recovering from these deviations is challenging, as they push the policy into unfamiliar state spaces where direct re-planning frequently destabilizes action sequences. We propose Back to the Familiar Future (B2FF), a recovery framework for foresight-driven VLAs that leverages future visual conditioning as a recovery interface. Before execution, the VLA generates a milestone bank of familiar future states conditioned on the clean initial observation. At recovery time, a recoverability-aware selector selects a recovery milestone from this bank and enforces it as a fixed visual goal. This enables the VLA to robustly map off-trajectory observations back to a familiar future. On failure-injected LIBERO, under controlled recovery timing aligned with the injected failure, B2FF increases the average success rate of a baseline VLA from 56.3% to 74.0%, demonstrating that pre-imagined milestones can guide recovery without fine-tuning the low-level action generator.

AI.tldr: B2FF is a recovery framework for VLA policies that uses pre-generated milestone banks of familiar future states to recover from execution deviations, improving success rates from 56.3% to 74.0% on failure-injected LIBERO without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: VLA policies drift off nominal trajectories during manipulation, and standard re-planning in unfamiliar state spaces destabilizes action sequences, creating a need for robust recovery without fine-tuning.
AI.method: B2FF pre-computes a milestone bank of familiar future states from the clean initial observation. At recovery time, a recoverability-aware selector picks a recovery milestone and enforces it as a fixed visual goal, enabling the VLA to map off-trajectory observations back to a familiar future.
AI.result: On failure-injected LIBERO with controlled recovery timing, B2FF raises average success rate from 56.3% to 74.0% for the baseline VLA.
AI.conclusion: Pre-imagined milestones serve as an effective recovery interface for foresight-driven VLAs, guiding recovery without requiring fine-tuning of the low-level action generator.

title: Towards Long-Horizon Vessel Trajectory and Destination Forecasting with Reasoning Large Language Models
comment: The IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC) 2026, Naples, Italy
summary: Long-horizon maritime trajectory prediction is important for shipping management, logistics planning, and maritime risk analysis, yet month-level forecasting remains insufficiently studied. Existing deep learning methods mainly focus on short- and mid-term coordinate extrapolation and often struggle to preserve route feasibility and destination correctness over extended horizons. This paper investigates joint long-horizon vessel trajectory and destination forecasting with reasoning-capable large language models, and develops a Maritime LLM post-training framework based on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR). An AIS-based benchmark is constructed with 60-day historical trajectories and 30-day forecasting horizons, where trajectories are converted into semantic textual representations for RL prompt construction. RLVR aligns LLMs with maritime forecasting objectives by enforcing physical validity, providing early-weighted trajectory supervision, and evaluating destination correctness through hierarchical matching and curriculum learning. Experimental results show that RLVR-trained LLMs substantially improve over zero-shot LLMs and representative deep learning baselines, especially on destination-related metrics. Among the evaluated RLVR-trained variants, 4B LLMs achieve the best overall performance, suggesting that reward-compatible optimization and task-specific capacity matching are more important than simply using larger 8B or 14B LLMs. The results also show that LSTM remains a strong deep learning baseline under limited fine-tuning data, while Transformer-style spatio-temporal models typically require larger datasets and richer structured inputs. Overall, this work advances semantic, verifier-aligned maritime forecasting for operational decision support.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an RLVR-based post-training framework for LLMs to perform long-horizon (30-day) maritime trajectory and destination prediction, outperforming zero-shot LLMs and deep learning baselines, with 4B LLMs achieving the best trade-off.
AI.motivation: Month-level maritime trajectory prediction remains understudied; existing deep learning methods focus on short/mid-term coordinate extrapolation and struggle with route feasibility and destination correctness over extended horizons.
AI.method: A Maritime LLM post-training framework using Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR). Trajectories (60-day history, 30-day forecast) are converted to semantic text representations. RLVR enforces physical validity, early-weighted trajectory supervision, and hierarchical destination matching via curriculum learning.
AI.result: RLVR-trained LLMs significantly outperform zero-shot LLMs and deep learning baselines, especially on destination metrics. 4B LLMs achieve the best overall performance, surpassing larger 8B/14B variants. LSTM remains a strong baseline under limited data; Transformer models require larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: Reward-compatible optimization and task-specific capacity matching are more important than simply scaling model size. The work advances semantic, verifier-aligned maritime forecasting for operational decision support.

title: VGP-Nav: Metric-Aware Visual Geometric Perception for Robot Navigation
summary: Reliable robotic navigation necessitates the seamless integration of accurate global localization and dense, metric-consistent obstacle perception. A common strategy to achieve these capabilities involves integrating diverse sensing modalities: cameras offer rich visual features for localization, while active sensors like LiDAR provide direct metric measurements. However, such multi-sensor configurations necessitate complex spatial-temporal calibration and increase deployment overhead. Although vision-only approaches offer a low-cost and scalable alternative, existing monocular visual systems typically struggle to simultaneously achieve efficient, globally consistent localization and dense, metric-consistent geometric perception. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{VGP-Nav}, a unified framework for \textit{Metric-Aware Visual Geometric Perception} that relies solely on monocular RGB input to jointly support metric localization and obstacle perception. Our key insight is to anchor localization-grounded visual geometry to physically meaningful scale constraints derived from ground-plane geometry, thereby providing a reliable metric reference for monocular perception. VGP-Nav resolves monocular scale ambiguity online and produces localization-grounded, metric obstacle representations that are directly applicable to downstream planning. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong generalization across diverse environments and successful deployment on real mobile robots, highlighting the practicality of our approach for scalable, low-cost, and safe autonomous navigation.

AI.tldr: VGP-Nav is a monocular RGB-only framework that achieves metric-aware visual geometric perception by anchoring localization to ground-plane geometry, enabling simultaneous global localization and dense metric obstacle perception for reliable robotic navigation without multi-sensor calibration.
AI.motivation: Existing robotic navigation typically requires multi-sensor setups (cameras + LiDAR) with complex calibration, while pure monocular vision systems struggle to jointly achieve globally consistent localization and dense metric perception due to scale ambiguity.
AI.method: VGP-Nav anchors localization-grounded visual geometry to physically meaningful scale constraints derived from ground-plane geometry, resolving monocular scale ambiguity online and producing metric obstacle representations directly usable for planning.
AI.result: Strong generalization across diverse environments and successful real-world deployment on mobile robots, demonstrating practicality for scalable, low-cost, safe autonomous navigation.
AI.conclusion: Monocular RGB-only input is sufficient for reliable metric localization and obstacle perception when grounded by geometric scale constraints, eliminating the need for multi-sensor configurations and complex calibration.

title: Extending Ontologies: From Dense Embeddings to Hybrid Quantum-Fuzzy Systems
summary: LLMs have revolutionized knowledge representation and retrieval, but lack the explicit modeling that knowledge ontologies possess. This paper surveys the ways that ontologies and knowledge graphs have been integrated with dense embedding algorithms. All hitherto attempts involve a trade-off between probabilistic and crisp inference. This paper proposes a novel frontier for devising knowledge representation systems that can simultaneously accommodate probabilistic and crisp inference in the same representation. To this effect, the paper proposes neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems as knowledge representation systems that accommodate both classical and contextual inference implemented through quantum-neural networks (QNN).

AI.tldr: This paper surveys ontology and knowledge graph integration with dense embeddings, identifies the trade-off between probabilistic and crisp inference, and proposes neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems using quantum-neural networks to accommodate both inference types simultaneously.
AI.motivation: LLMs lack explicit knowledge modeling that ontologies provide; existing attempts at combining ontologies with dense embeddings involve a trade-off between probabilistic and crisp inference.
AI.method: Surveys existing ontology/knowledge graph integration with dense embeddings; proposes neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems implementing quantum-neural networks (QNN) to bridge probabilistic and crisp inference.
AI.result: Identifies a fundamental trade-off in prior work; proposes a novel frontier where both inference types coexist via QNN-based neuro-quantum-fuzzy representations.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-quantum-fuzzy systems offer a promising direction for unified knowledge representation supporting both classical (crisp) and contextual (probabilistic) inference.

title: VAIC: Vision-Guided Humanoid Agile Object Interaction Control via Decoupled Commands
summary: Humanoid robots hold immense potential for real-world assistance, yet agile interaction with objects in unstructured environments demands tightly coupled whole-body coordination. Despite recent advancements, current controllers face a critical deployment gap. They rely heavily on dense reference trajectories and perfect state observability, which inherently limits physical generalization. We present Vision Guided Agile Interaction Control (VAIC), a unified framework that bridges this gap by operating exclusively on onboard depth, historical proprioception, and a decoupled user command interface. VAIC employs a two-stage distillation paradigm. First, a privileged teacher policy masters diverse interaction skills using precise object kinematics and exact environmental states. Second, a deployable student policy distills these capabilities by replacing full body tracking with velocity targets across multiple axes and an interaction indicator for each frame. The student utilizes a recurrent object adaptation module to implicitly infer unobservable object dynamics from raw depth streams and proprioception. Evaluations and real-world deployments on the humanoid robot demonstrate that a single VAIC policy successfully executes highly diverse dynamic tasks. These tasks include box carrying, cart interaction, and skateboarding, consistently outperforming baselines and advancing autonomous humanoid deployment.

AI.tldr: VAIC is a unified framework for humanoid robot whole-body coordination that uses onboard depth, proprioception, and user commands to perform diverse dynamic tasks via a two-stage privileged teacher and deployable student distillation paradigm with recurrent object adaptation.
AI.motivation: Current humanoid controllers rely on dense reference trajectories and perfect state observability, creating a deployment gap that limits physical generalization in unstructured environments.
AI.method: Two-stage distillation paradigm: (1) a privileged teacher policy masters interaction skills using precise object kinematics and exact environmental states; (2) a deployable student policy distills capabilities using velocity targets, an interaction indicator, and a recurrent object adaptation module to infer unobservable object dynamics from raw depth streams and proprioception.
AI.result: A single VAIC policy successfully executes diverse dynamic tasks—box carrying, cart interaction, and skateboarding—on a real humanoid robot, consistently outperforming baselines.
AI.conclusion: VAIC advances autonomous humanoid deployment by enabling agile whole-body interaction with objects using only onboard sensing, bridging the gap between simulation-trained policies and real-world deployment.

title: ConMem: Structured Memory-Guided Adaptation in Training-Free Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Recent advances have improved the adaptive capabilities of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) through memory-, skill-, and learning-based approaches, yet these approaches remain challenged by noisy trajectories, insufficient modeling of memory-skill relations, and reliance on additional training or high-quality supervision. To address these limitations, we propose ConMem, a relation-aware and training-free framework that enables efficient multi-agent adaptation through cross-experience coordination. Specifically, ConMem distills historical interaction trajectories into structured memory cards to capture reusable strategies and cues, organizing them into a relation-aware memory graph. At runtime, ConMem retrieves cards according to task needs and coordinates them through the card graph to resolve strategy conflicts and recover their dependencies. Combined, these modules yield structured and relation-aware guidance, enabling robust, lightweight adaptation in multi-agent systems without additional training. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks and mainstream MAS architectures show consistent gains over existing memory architectures, with improved inference-time efficiency through pruning more than 50% of expanded candidates and reducing planning overhead by over 80%. Our codes are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ConMemCode

AI.tldr: ConMem is a training-free, relation-aware framework that improves LLM-based multi-agent adaptation by distilling trajectories into structured memory cards organized in a graph, enabling efficient cross-experience coordination without additional training, achieving over 50% candidate pruning and 80% planning overhead reduction.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent adaptation approaches (memory-, skill-, learning-based) suffer from noisy trajectories, poor modeling of memory-skill relations, and reliance on additional training or high-quality supervision, limiting their efficiency and robustness.
AI.method: ConMem distills historical interaction trajectories into structured memory cards capturing reusable strategies and cues, organizes them into a relation-aware memory graph, retrieves relevant cards at runtime based on task needs, and coordinates them via the graph to resolve conflicts and recover dependencies—all without additional training.
AI.result: Consistent gains over existing memory architectures across multiple benchmarks and mainstream MAS architectures; prunes over 50% of expanded candidates and reduces planning overhead by over 80%.
AI.conclusion: ConMem provides a robust, lightweight, and training-free solution for multi-agent adaptation through structured, relation-aware cross-experience coordination, significantly improving both effectiveness and inference-time efficiency.

title: Dual Quaternion-Based Unscented Kalman Filter with Visual Inertial Odometry for Navigation in GPS-Denied Environments
summary: Reliable navigation in GPS-denied environments remains a fundamental challenge in robotics, aerospace, and autonomous vehicle applications. This paper presents a Dual Quaternion-Based Unscented Kalman Filter (DQUKF) equipped with a Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) algorithm for accurate state estimation enabling navigation in GPS denied locations. The proposed framework formulates the DQUKF in an error state manner, where the nominal pose is represented by a unit dual quaternion and the local pose error is represented by a 6-dimensional twistor parameterization used for sigma point generation, covariance propagation, and measurement correction. In parallel, the VIO algorithm tracks features across image frames, synchronizes measurements between the IMU and camera, and provides visual constraints that complement inertial propagation. Simulation results on the EuRoC MAV dataset show that the proposed DQUKF converges under high initialization uncertainty and achieves a position RMSE of 0.2584~m in the difficult flight sequence, outperforming the benchmark filters.

AI.tldr: A Dual Quaternion-Based Unscented Kalman Filter (DQUKF) with Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) is proposed for GPS-denied navigation, achieving 0.2584 m position RMSE on the EuRoC MAV dataset, outperforming benchmark filters.
AI.motivation: Reliable navigation in GPS-denied environments remains a fundamental challenge in robotics, aerospace, and autonomous vehicle applications.
AI.method: The DQUKF is formulated in an error state manner: nominal pose represented by a unit dual quaternion, local pose error by a 6-dimensional twistor parameterization for sigma point generation, covariance propagation, and measurement correction. A VIO algorithm tracks features across image frames, synchronizes IMU and camera measurements, and provides visual constraints.
AI.result: On the EuRoC MAV dataset, the DQUKF converges under high initialization uncertainty and achieves a position RMSE of 0.2584 m in the difficult flight sequence, outperforming benchmark filters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DQUKF with VIO provides accurate state estimation enabling navigation in GPS-denied locations.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Mathematical Reasoning: An Integrated Survey of Language Models, Neuro-symbolic Systems, and Verified Discovery
summary: Mathematical reasoning has long served as a stringent test of machine intelligence; over the past decade, it has moved from a niche problem within NLP to one of the most consequential AI frontiers. This survey provides a unified account of the field's evolution, from early rule-based math word problem (MWP) solvers and template-driven geometry systems, through neural expression generation and LLM prompting, to contemporary reasoning models, multi-agent systems, neuro-symbolic theorem provers, and verified discovery workflows. We organize the landscape along four axes: (i) informal reasoning over text and diagrams, spanning MWP solving, multimodal geometry, and VLMs; (ii) formal reasoning in proof assistants, including autoformalization, tactic prediction, compiler-guided repair, and proof search; (iii) mathematical discovery, where systems propose constructions, improve bounds, or assist attacks on open problems; and (iv) the inference and training-time techniques, including CoT prompting, tool use, process reward models, and RLVR, that increasingly connect generation with verification. We catalog major benchmarks across grade-school arithmetic, competition mathematics, geometry, formal proving, multimodal and multilingual reasoning, and expert evaluation, and we examine benchmark saturation, contamination, reporting mismatches, and the distinction between pass@1, majority voting, and verifier-assisted pass@$k$. We critically assess failure modes: brittleness under perturbation, reward hacking, multimodal grounding failures, fragile formalization, and the energy cost of reasoning-scale inference. Drawing on recent perspectives from working mathematicians, we identify future directions centered on verified-discovery workflows, reasoning efficiency, and infrastructure to make AI-assisted formalization broadly usable. Companion materials: https://github.com/Starscream-11813/awesome-AI4Math.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey of AI for mathematical reasoning, tracing its evolution from early rule-based solvers to modern reasoning models, multi-agent systems, and verified discovery workflows, organized along four axes: informal reasoning, formal reasoning, mathematical discovery, and inference/training-time techniques.
AI.motivation: Mathematical reasoning serves as a stringent test of machine intelligence and has become a major AI frontier; a unified account of the field's rapid evolution is needed to organize the vast body of work spanning informal and formal reasoning, discovery, and training techniques.
AI.method: The survey organizes the landscape along four axes: (i) informal reasoning over text and diagrams, (ii) formal reasoning in proof assistants, (iii) mathematical discovery (proposing constructions, improving bounds, attacking open problems), and (iv) inference and training-time techniques (CoT, tool use, process reward models, RLVR). It also catalogs benchmarks and critically assesses failure modes.
AI.result: Catalogs major benchmarks across grade-school arithmetic, competition math, geometry, formal proving, multimodal/multilingual reasoning, and expert evaluation. Identifies failure modes including brittleness under perturbation, reward hacking, multimodal grounding failures, fragile formalization, and energy costs of reasoning-scale inference.
AI.conclusion: Future directions center on verified-discovery workflows, reasoning efficiency, and infrastructure for broadly usable AI-assisted formalization. Companion materials are available on GitHub.

title: KPGrasp: Scalable Keypoint Flow Matching for Dexterous Grasp Generation
summary: Generating high-quality dexterous grasps remains challenging for learning-based methods, which often depend on carefully tuned contact losses or costly contact-based test-time refinement. We present KPGrasp, a flow-matching framework that learns dexterous grasp priors from large-scale data rather than relying on contact losses or contact-based test-time refinement. KPGrasp couples an all-Euclidean 3D hand-keypoint parameterization with a simple yet scalable Transformer flow model. The parameterization avoids the drawbacks of the conventional mixed SE(3) pose and joint-angle output space, expresses grasps in the same frame as the object point cloud, and thus enables native spatial reasoning; the Transformer flow model is trained with only the standard flow-matching loss and scales effectively with data, model capacity, and batch size. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on two simulation benchmarks. On the Dexonomy benchmark, it reaches a 76.3% grasp success rate, improving over the strongest directly comparable baseline by 47.4% while reducing penetration depth to 2.4 mm. The same model also achieves the best average performance on the DexGrasp Anything benchmark without fine-tuning. For batched inference, KPGrasp requires only 0.032 s per grasp. Finally, real-world experiments on 20 diverse objects demonstrate that the pipeline can be deployed in a real-world setup.

AI.tldr: KPGrasp is a flow-matching framework that learns dexterous grasp priors from large-scale data using an all-Euclidean 3D hand-keypoint parameterization and a Transformer flow model, achieving SOTA results on simulation benchmarks (76.3% success rate, 2.4 mm penetration depth) and real-world deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing learning-based dexterous grasping methods rely heavily on carefully tuned contact losses or costly contact-based test-time refinement, which limits scalability and generalization.
AI.method: KPGrasp couples an all-Euclidean 3D hand-keypoint parameterization (avoiding mixed SE(3) pose and joint-angle spaces) with a Transformer flow model trained using only the standard flow-matching loss. This parameterization expresses grasps in the same coordinate frame as the object point cloud, enabling native spatial reasoning.
AI.result: 76.3% grasp success rate on Dexonomy (47.4% improvement over strongest baseline), 2.4 mm penetration depth reduction; best average performance on DexGrasp Anything; 0.032 s per grasp for batched inference; successful real-world deployment on 20 diverse objects.
AI.conclusion: KPGrasp demonstrates that learning grasp priors from data via flow matching, without contact losses or test-time refinement, is both effective and scalable for high-quality dexterous grasping in simulation and the real world.

title: Structure-Conditioned Actor-Critic Branches for Quality-Diversity Reinforcement Learning
summary: Quality-diversity reinforcement learning (QD-RL) aims to construct policy repertoires that contain both high-performing and behaviorally diverse policies. Existing QD-RL methods mainly diversify policy instances after rollout evaluation or use learned value information to improve policy quality and behavior targeting, while the learning branches that generate candidate policies remain less explored. This paper proposes SV-QD-RL, a structure-value coupled framework that represents each candidate as a structure-conditioned actor-critic branch. Each branch contains an actor, a structural mask, a branch-specific critic, a replay state, and evaluation attributes including behavior, return, sparsity, and value profile. The structural mask defines the actor subspace in which the branch learns, while the branch-specific critic and replay state shape its value-learning trajectory. A branch-aware QD archive then evaluates and retains branches according to behavioral quality, structural footprint, and value-profile information. Experiments on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks show that SV-QD-RL constructs policy repertoires with strong archive quality and behaviorally useful diversity. Ablation and diagnostic analyses further indicate that structural conditioning, critic differentiation, and memory-consistent refinement make complementary contributions to behavioral specialization. Schedule-aware repertoire evaluation shows that the learned archive provides selectable policy alternatives under changing behavior-level requirements. These results suggest that coupling actor structure with branch-specific value learning is an effective mechanism for generating diverse QD-RL policy repertoires.

AI.tldr: SV-QD-RL introduces a structure-value coupled framework where each candidate policy is a separate actor-critic branch with its own structural mask, critic, and replay state, leading to improved archive quality and behavioral diversity in MuJoCo tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing QD-RL methods diversify policy instances mainly after rollout evaluation or via learned value information, but the learning branches that generate candidate policies remain underexplored.
AI.method: Each candidate is a structure-conditioned actor-critic branch with a structural mask (defining actor subspace), branch-specific critic, replay state, and evaluation attributes (behavior, return, sparsity, value profile). A branch-aware QD archive evaluates and retains branches based on behavioral quality, structural footprint, and value-profile information.
AI.result: SV-QD-RL constructs policy repertoires with strong archive quality and behaviorally useful diversity on MuJoCo continuous-control tasks. Ablation shows structural conditioning, critic differentiation, and memory-consistent refinement contribute complementarily to behavioral specialization.
AI.conclusion: Coupling actor structure with branch-specific value learning is an effective mechanism for generating diverse QD-RL policy repertoires.

title: TORL-VLA: Tactile Guided Online Reinforcement Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful framework for robotic manipulation, and recent studies have introduced tactile or force feedback into VLAs to address contact-rich tasks. However, these models are typically deployed as offline policies. When contact conditions shift from the training distribution, the policy cannot perform online adaptation, leading to problems such as inappropriate contact forces and inefficient retries. Therefore, we propose TORL-VLA, a tactile-guided online reinforcement learning framework that couples tactile feedback with policy refinement for contact-rich manipulation. Our method introduces a tactile-derived wrench-aware VLA to predict reference actions and future wrench sequences, while a lightweight online RL module is used to refine the reference actions. To stabilize learning from mixed exploratory policy-generated and human-intervention data, we introduce an intervention-censored critic that prevents post-intervention success from being wrongly credited to policy-generated actions preceding intervention. Real-robot experiments on long-horizon contact-rich tasks, including latch manipulation, coffee-cup placement, and egg handling, show that TORL-VLA improves success rates at both subtask and full-task levels, as well as time-bounded execution efficiency over strong baselines.

AI.tldr: TORL-VLA is a tactile-guided online reinforcement learning framework that couples tactile feedback with policy refinement for contact-rich manipulation, using a wrench-aware VLA to predict actions and an online RL module with intervention-censored critic for adaptation, achieving improved success rates and efficiency on real-robot tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models with tactile/force feedback are deployed as offline policies and fail to adapt online when contact conditions shift from training distribution, causing inappropriate contact forces and inefficient retries.
AI.method: Proposes TORL-VLA with: (1) a tactile-derived wrench-aware VLA predicting reference actions and future wrench sequences, (2) a lightweight online RL module for refining reference actions, and (3) an intervention-censored critic to prevent credit assignment issues from mixed exploratory and human-intervention data.
AI.result: Real-robot experiments on latch manipulation, coffee-cup placement, and egg handling show improved success rates at subtask and full-task levels, and better time-bounded execution efficiency over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Coupling tactile feedback with online RL enables VLA models to adapt online to shifting contact conditions, significantly improving performance on contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: RAILS: Verification-Native Clearing For Agentic Commerce
summary:
Autonomous agents negotiate, purchase, deploy code, and move funds, but no neutral mechanism determines whether they
  met their delegated obligation, who is responsible when they did not, or which settlement action follows. This is the
  agentic clearing problem. Tool protocols (MCP), inter-agent communication (A2A), payment rails (x402), mandate and
  network agent protocols (AP2, Visa, Mastercard), and settlement-risk standards each assume that determination and none
  produce it.
  Clearing is the missing primitive. Payment is not clearing. Authorization is not clearing. LLM-as-judge evaluation is
  not clearing. Settlement-risk escrow is not clearing: it consumes clearing decisions.
  RAILS (Real-Time Agent Integrity & Ledger Settlement) is the integrity and clearing layer for agentic commerce,
  spanning a per-output reliability score, a published reliability record, and a clearing function that consumes them.
  The clearing protocol at its core closes that gap. Seven primitives (Obligation Object, Evidence Envelope,
  Verification Mesh, Clearing Decision, Settlement Instruction, Clearing Passport, Finality Rules), bound by a formal
  model of admissibility-graded verification, together yield a soundness property: no financially material settlement is
  supported by evidence below the obligation's admissibility floor. The property is falsifiable against the spec. We
  are not aware of a prior agent-commerce verification mechanism that states a property of this kind. The approaches
  nearest to it emit a pass, a delivery guarantee, a bare score, or an equilibrium.
  This paper specifies that clearing protocol.

AI.tldr: RAILS introduces a clearing protocol for autonomous agent commerce, providing an integrity layer with a reliability scoring system, evidence verification mesh, and formal settlement rules that ensure no financially material settlement occurs below an admissibility floor.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous agent systems (MCP, A2A, Visa, Mastercard, etc.) lack a neutral mechanism to determine obligation fulfillment, assign responsibility, or trigger settlement actions—this is the "agentic clearing problem" that no existing protocol solves.
AI.method: RAILS defines seven primitives (Obligation Object, Evidence Envelope, Verification Mesh, Clearing Decision, Settlement Instruction, Clearing Passport, Finality Rules) governed by a formal model of admissibility-graded verification, yielding a soundness property that is falsifiable against the specification.
AI.result: The protocol achieves a soundness property: no financially material settlement is supported by evidence below the obligation's admissibility floor. This is a novel property not previously stated in agent-commerce verification mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: RAILS fills the missing "clearing" primitive in agentic commerce, spanning per-output reliability scores, published reliability records, and a clearing function, with a formal guarantee against insufficiently-evidenced settlements.

title: Taming Perception Jitter: Uncertainty-Aware LiDAR Object Detection for Reliable Motion Classification
summary: Reliable motion classification is critical for autonomous driving, as false dynamic predictions of static objects can cascade into unnecessary planner interventions. Unstable bounding box predictions can lead to spurious velocity estimates in tracking and falsely predicted trajectories. We present a deployment-friendly mitigation strategy that augments a 3D object detector with aleatoric uncertainty estimates and applies a two-sample z-test over short observation windows to separate true motion from jitter. Integrated into Autoware with minimal changes, the approach reuses existing data association for minimal compute overhead. Empirical results show parity with velocity thresholding on nuScenes, but substantially fewer false dynamic predictions and unnecessary stops in real-world test drives, explained by the presence of an intermediate jitter band in the recorded data that speed-only rules misclassify. This demonstrates that uncertainty-aware detection and lightweight statistical testing can deliver practical performance gains for autonomous driving in noisier real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A lightweight uncertainty-aware 3D detector with statistical z-testing reduces false motion classifications and unnecessary stops in autonomous driving by distinguishing true motion from bounding box jitter, outperforming simple velocity thresholding in real-world noisy settings.
AI.motivation: Reliable motion classification is critical for autonomous driving; false dynamic predictions of static objects cause unnecessary planner interventions. Unstable bounding box predictions lead to spurious velocity estimates and falsely predicted trajectories.
AI.method: Augments a 3D object detector with aleatoric uncertainty estimates and applies a two-sample z-test over short observation windows to separate true motion from jitter. Integrated into Autoware with minimal changes, reusing existing data association for minimal compute overhead.
AI.result: Parity with velocity thresholding on nuScenes, but substantially fewer false dynamic predictions and unnecessary stops in real-world test drives, due to an intermediate jitter band that speed-only rules misclassify.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-aware detection and lightweight statistical testing deliver practical performance gains for autonomous driving in noisier real-world settings.

title: Bridging Expert Knowledge and Automated Feature Engineering via Self-Evolution
summary: In high-stakes settings such as brand compliance, clinical care, and content moderation, machine learning cannot be deployed as opaque oracles: practitioners inspect the features driving model decisions, and models must leverage the expert documentation governing these domains. In practice, the data arrives as unstructured content, and features extracted from it must be interpretable, discriminative, and aligned with what experts consider important. Existing methods fall short: they target tabular inputs, lack demonstrated expert alignment, and cannot operationalize qualitative criteria such as 'maintain professional tone' into precise features. We present FEST (Feature Engineering with Self-evolving Trees), combining dual-stream feature generation (semantic and deterministic), semantic deduplication, and tree-guided iterative evolution to discover auditable features from raw text and images. FEST leads in 17 of 20 classifier-task combinations across brand classification, content authenticity detection, and stress detection, with a mean gain of 4.2 pp over the strongest baseline across five classifiers. An LLM-as-judge evaluation shows FEST achieves 60-80% coverage of expert-designed brand features at strict semantic-alignment thresholds, corroborated by a human expert study rating features highly on relevance, clarity, and actionability. When seeded with expert guidelines, FEST refines qualitative criteria into operational features, improving accuracy by 6-12 pp on average across brands. To enable systematic evaluation of expert alignment in automated feature engineering, we release BrandGuide, the first dataset pairing expert-designed features with 1M+ assets across 2,683 brands. By grounding feature engineering in expert knowledge, FEST opens a practical pathway for interpretable ML in domains demanding human oversight.

AI.tldr: FEST (Feature Engineering with Self-evolving Trees) is a method that automatically discovers auditable, interpretable features from raw text and images by combining dual-stream feature generation, semantic deduplication, and tree-guided iterative evolution. It outperforms baselines in 17/20 classifier-task combinations (mean +4.2 pp), achieves 60-80% coverage of expert-designed features, and improves accuracy by 6-12 pp when seeded with expert guidelines. The paper also releases BrandGuide, the first dataset pairing expert features with 1M+ assets across 2,683 brands.
AI.motivation: In high-stakes domains (brand compliance, clinical care, content moderation), ML models must be interpretable and aligned with expert knowledge. Existing feature engineering methods fail because they target tabular data, lack expert alignment, and cannot operationalize qualitative criteria into precise features.
AI.method: FEST uses dual-stream feature generation (semantic and deterministic), semantic deduplication, and tree-guided iterative evolution to discover auditable features from raw text and images. It can also be seeded with expert guidelines to refine qualitative criteria into operational features.
AI.result: FEST leads in 17 of 20 classifier-task combinations with mean gain of 4.2 pp over strongest baseline across five classifiers. LLM-as-judge evaluation shows 60-80% coverage of expert-designed brand features. Human expert study rates features highly on relevance, clarity, and actionability. When seeded with expert guidelines, accuracy improves by 6-12 pp on average across brands.
AI.conclusion: By grounding feature engineering in expert knowledge, FEST provides a practical pathway for interpretable ML in domains demanding human oversight. The release of BrandGuide enables systematic evaluation of expert alignment in automated feature engineering.

title: MosaicIMU: Composing Carrier Experts for Generalizable Neural Inertial Odometry
summary: Robust inertial odometry is essential for various carriers when external sensing is unreliable. Learning-based methods reduce integration drift by capturing local motion priors, but these methods often remain tied to a particular carrier, limiting generalization across heterogeneous platforms. We present MosaicIMU, a carrier-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) pretraining-and-adaptation framework for generalizable neural inertial odometry. MosaicIMU uses a prototype-based router to compose carrier-specific expert features, decodes local velocity and uncertainty constraints, and integrates them with a history-aware EKF. For unseen domain adaptation, it freezes the pretrained base model and learns a new lightweight expert residual branch. For edge-deployment, it further reuses the router to select informative online samples for efficient incremental updates. Experiments show that MosaicIMU consistently outperforms learning-based baselines, reducing average ATE and RTE-10s by 40% and 34%, respectively. These results highlight that MosaicIMU provides a scalable pretraining-to-deployment paradigm for generalizable and adaptive neural inertial odometry.

AI.tldr: MosaicIMU is a carrier-conditioned Mixture-of-Experts pretraining-and-adaptation framework for generalizable neural inertial odometry that uses prototype-based routing to compose carrier-specific features, achieves 40% ATE and 34% RTE-10s reduction, and supports unseen domain adaptation and edge deployment.
AI.motivation: Learning-based inertial odometry methods suffer from poor generalization across heterogeneous carriers (e.g., drones, vehicles, pedestrians) because they are trained for specific platforms. A generalizable framework that can adapt to different carriers without retraining the full model is needed.
AI.method: MosaicIMU employs (1) a prototype-based router to compose carrier-specific expert features via MoE; (2) decoding of local velocity and uncertainty constraints integrated with a history-aware EKF; (3) frozen pretrained base + lightweight expert residual branch for unseen domain adaptation; (4) router-guided online sample selection for efficient edge deployment incremental updates.
AI.result: MosaicIMU consistently outperforms learning-based baselines, reducing average ATE by 40% and RTE-10s by 34% across heterogeneous platforms.
AI.conclusion: MosaicIMU provides a scalable pretraining-to-deployment paradigm for generalizable and adaptive neural inertial odometry, demonstrating strong cross-carrier generalization and efficient adaptation.

title: Q-Delta: Beyond Key-Value Associative State Evolution
summary: Linear attention reformulates sequence modeling as recurrent state evolution, enabling efficient linear-time inference. Under the key-value associative paradigm, existing approaches restrict the role of the query to the readout operation, decoupling it from state evolution. We show that query-conditioned state readout induces a structured value prediction over accumulated memory that complements key-based retrieval. Based on this insight, we propose Q-Delta, a query-aware delta rule that integrates mixed key-query prediction errors into state evolution, enabling jointly corrective dynamics while preserving delta-rule efficiency. We establish stability guarantees for the resulting dynamics and derive a hardware-efficient chunkwise-parallel formulation with a custom Triton implementation. Empirical results demonstrate stable optimization, competitive throughput, and consistent improvements over strong baselines on language modeling and long-context retrieval tasks.

AI.tldr: Q-Delta introduces a query-aware delta rule that integrates mixed key-query prediction errors into state evolution for linear attention, achieving jointly corrective dynamics with efficiency guarantees and consistent improvements on language modeling and long-context retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing linear attention approaches decouple the query from state evolution, restricting it to readout operations only. This limits the model's ability to leverage query information for corrective state updates during recurrent processing.
AI.method: Q-Delta proposes a query-aware delta rule that incorporates mixed key-query prediction errors into state evolution, combining query-conditioned readout with key-based retrieval. The method includes stability guarantees, a chunkwise-parallel formulation, and a custom Triton implementation for hardware efficiency.
AI.result: Stable optimization, competitive throughput, and consistent improvements over strong baselines on language modeling and long-context retrieval tasks.
AI.conclusion: Query-conditioned state readout induces structured value prediction that complements key-based retrieval, and jointly corrective dynamics can be efficiently integrated into delta-rule linear attention without sacrificing efficiency.

title: ReGIL: Retrieval-Guided Imitation Learning from a Single Demonstration
summary: Learning robot manipulation policies with deep neural networks from a single demonstration remains highly challenging, as even small deviations from the demonstrated trajectory can quickly compound into failure, while collecting substantial online interaction data is costly. We propose ReGIL, a retrieval-guided imitation learning framework that treats a single demonstration as an external memory. ReGIL repeatedly queries this static memory throughout training to simultaneously guide exploration, generate the regularization buffer, and construct rewards. Specifically, it computes rewards through local temporal alignment between the current trajectory and the retrieved segment, providing step-wise and informative feedback for policy improvement. We evaluate ReGIL on robotic manipulation tasks from the LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks under the single demonstration setting. ReGIL outperforms prior baselines in both success rate and training efficiency. In real-robot experiments, using only one demonstration and less than one hour of online training, ReGIL achieves over 75% success rate across three manipulation tasks with randomness in both initial robot pose and target position. These results demonstrate that leveraging the single demonstration as reusable memory can provide more than static supervision for efficient robot learning. More details can be found on our website: https://regil2026.github.io/

AI.tldr: ReGIL is a retrieval-guided imitation learning framework that treats a single demonstration as an external memory, using it to guide exploration, generate regularization buffers, and construct rewards via local temporal alignment, achieving superior performance on robotic manipulation tasks with minimal data.
AI.motivation: Learning robot manipulation policies from a single demonstration is highly challenging because small deviations from the demonstrated trajectory compound into failure, and collecting substantial online interaction data is costly. The goal is to enable efficient robot learning without requiring large demonstration datasets or extensive online data collection.
AI.method: ReGIL treats a single demonstration as an external memory, repeatedly querying it throughout training to: (1) guide exploration, (2) generate the regularization buffer, and (3) construct rewards. Rewards are computed via local temporal alignment between the current trajectory and the retrieved demonstration segment, providing step-wise and informative feedback.
AI.result: On LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks under the single demonstration setting, ReGIL outperforms prior baselines in both success rate and training efficiency. In real-robot experiments, using only one demonstration and less than one hour of online training, ReGIL achieves over 75% success rate across three manipulation tasks with randomness in both initial robot pose and target position.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging a single demonstration as reusable memory provides more than static supervision for efficient robot learning, enabling effective policy improvement with minimal data.

title: STAR: Rethinking MoE Routing as Structure-Aware Subspace Learning
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales model capacity efficiently by selectively routing inputs to a specialized subset of experts. However, input-expert specialization, the core motivation of MoE, critically depends on whether the router is actually aware of input structure. In practice, MoE routing is typically implemented as a shallow linear projection with limited awareness of input representation, which often leads to unstable routing. We propose STAR, a Structure Aware Routing that rethinks MoE routing as a subspace learning problem by augmenting standard learnable routing with an evolving principal subspace that tracks dominant input structure via Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA). By aligning routing decisions directly with input structure, STAR enables stable expert specialization. We evaluate STAR on controlled synthetic setup and large-scale language and vision tasks, where it consistently improves routing quality and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines. Moreover, optional test-time subspace updates further enhance routing robustness and generalization under input distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: STAR proposes a Structure Aware Routing method for MoE that replaces shallow linear routing with subspace learning via Generalized Hebbian Algorithm, enabling stable expert specialization by aligning routing decisions with input structure.
AI.motivation: Standard MoE routing uses shallow linear projections with limited input awareness, causing unstable routing and poor input-expert specialization, which undermines the core motivation of MoE.
AI.method: STAR augments standard learnable routing with an evolving principal subspace that tracks dominant input structure using the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA), reformulating MoE routing as a subspace learning problem.
AI.result: STAR consistently improves routing quality and downstream performance over strong MoE baselines on synthetic, language, and vision tasks. Optional test-time subspace updates further enhance robustness under distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Aligning routing decisions with input structure via subspace learning achieves stable expert specialization and improved generalization, validating the importance of structure-aware routing in MoE.

title: Harness Engineering for Physical AI: Robot Middleware Is the Harness Layer
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Big Ideas track submission to the 27th ACM/IFIP International Middleware Conference (Middleware 2026)
summary: Robot middleware faces a new role in the era of Physical AI. Learned policies, planners, and vision-language-action (VLA) models now enter deployed robots as causal participants on the control path, but the layer that integrates them with timing, scheduling, and network has not been named. Recent language-agent work names this layer the harness, the external system that mediates tools, manages state, bounds resources, and records execution. The robotics community has not yet adopted this framing, and we propose that robot middleware is that harness. A Physical AI harness differs from a software harness in where it intervenes. A software harness mediates at tool-call boundaries. A Physical AI harness must mediate at control, computing, and communication simultaneously, because a learned policy's output crosses all three: its commands shift the trajectory, its inference time shifts the schedule, and its payload shifts the bandwidth. Robot middleware is the lowest robot-stack layer with mediating abstractions over all three, so it is best positioned to compose their enforcement. It already provides most of what a harness needs but lacks the enforcement for an AI model. We name this missing enforcement as three functions: Projection gates each output at emission, Isolation bounds the model's execution and transmission slot, and Transfer falls back to a verified baseline when checks fail. Each appears today as hand-built application code in deployed robot systems, built on surfaces robot middleware already provides. Robot middleware should host them not as the best single-axis enforcer but as the layer that composes all three. We sketch this as a ROS 2 Harness Profile, a deployment artifact that carries an AI model's declared output region, inference budget, and operating regime while the middleware enforces them across ROS 2, DDS, and Zenoh.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that robot middleware should serve as the "harness" for Physical AI systems—mediating learned policies, planners, and VLA models across control, computing, and communication axes—and introduces three missing enforcement functions (Projection, Isolation, Transfer) that middleware should natively compose, sketched as a ROS 2 Harness Profile.
AI.motivation: As learned policies, planners, and VLA models become causal participants in robot control paths, existing middleware lacks a named role and enforcement mechanisms to mediate their outputs across timing, scheduling, and networking dimensions. The robotics community has not adopted the "harness" framing from language-agent work.
AI.method: The paper identifies the gap by comparing software harnesses (tool-call boundaries) with Physical AI harness requirements (control, computing, communication simultaneously). It defines three enforcement functions: Projection (gating outputs at emission), Isolation (bounding model execution and transmission slots), and Transfer (falling back to a verified baseline). It sketches a ROS 2 Harness Profile carrying declared output region, inference budget, and operating regime.
AI.result: Robot middleware already provides most harness primitives but lacks AI-specific enforcement. The three functions (Projection, Isolation, Transfer) currently exist as ad-hoc application code. The proposed ROS 2 Harness Profile demonstrates how middleware can natively compose all three enforcement axes.
AI.conclusion: Robot middleware should be the composable enforcement layer for Physical AI, hosting Projection, Isolation, and Transfer natively rather than leaving them as hand-built application code. The ROS 2 Harness Profile provides a concrete deployment artifact for this vision.

title: Momentum for Reasoning: Dense Intrinsic Signals in Policy Optimization
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for eliciting long-chain reasoning in large language models. However, existing methods based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) rely on a binary outcome reward, which induces two structural failure modes: Zero-Advantage Collapse, in which all rollouts in a group share the same outcome and the gradient vanishes, and Hallucinated Certainty, in which the model becomes increasingly confident on incorrect rollouts late in training. We address both modes by densifying the reward with intrinsic signals computed entirely from the policy's own conditional probabilities, and propose ISPO (Intrinsic Signal Policy Optimization, which combines a sequence-level signal measuring how informative the thinking trajectory is for the final answer, with a token-level directional reward whose hallucinated-certainty hinge penalizes confidently-wrong predictions at critical decision tokens. Across three base models and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ISPO consistently outperforms competitive baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest benchmarks where zero-advantage collapse is most frequent, and training-dynamics diagnostics confirm that both failure modes are decreased.

AI.tldr: ISPO (Intrinsic Signal Policy Optimization) enhances RLVR for LLMs by densifying binary outcome rewards with intrinsic signals from the policy's own probabilities, fixing Zero-Advantage Collapse and Hallucinated Certainty, and outperforming baselines on math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR methods (e.g., GRPO) use binary outcome rewards that cause two failure modes: Zero-Advantage Collapse (gradient vanishes when all rollouts share the same outcome) and Hallucinated Certainty (model becomes overconfident on incorrect rollouts late in training).
AI.method: ISPO densifies the reward via two intrinsic signals computed from the policy's own conditional probabilities: (1) a sequence-level signal measuring how informative the thinking trajectory is for the final answer, and (2) a token-level directional reward with a hallucinated-certainty hinge that penalizes confidently-wrong predictions at critical decision tokens.
AI.result: Across three base models and five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ISPO consistently outperforms competitive baselines, with largest gains on the hardest benchmarks where zero-advantage collapse is most frequent. Training-dynamics diagnostics confirm both failure modes are decreased.
AI.conclusion: Densifying binary outcome rewards with intrinsic policy signals effectively mitigates structural failure modes in RLVR, leading to improved long-chain reasoning in LLMs, especially on challenging problems.

title: Dense Force Estimation with an Event-based Optical Tactile Sensor
summary: Humans rely on spatially dense, geometry and force-aware tactile feedback at high temporal resolution for dexterous manipulation. While vision-based tactile sensors enable dense force estimation, they are limited by camera frame rates, motion blur, and data bandwidth. Event-based optical tactile sensors offer an attractive alternative with microsecond temporal resolution and low motion blur, but existing methods are restricted to predicting only net forces. We introduce the first framework for dense 3D force field reconstruction using event-based optical tactile sensors.
